en: The Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi-tantra: The Empowerment of the Miraculous Transformation of the Buddha’s Enlightenment,
The Lotus Womb Matrix, The Banner of Bodhi, The Universal Treasury of Mantras,
The Extensive Accomplishment Yoga, Volume One.
The Śramaṇa Fazun of Qinglong Monastery, desiring to form this bond, respectfully addresses the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time:

"We, the dull-witted ordinary beings of the lower grade, though we hold this seal, are like mosquitoes and ants attempting to grasp Mount Sumeru; we fear we lack the necessary power. We only pray that the Buddhas will grant us their protection, enabling us to attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, so that by binding and holding this seal, we may possess power equal to that of the Buddhas."
I prostrate to Vairocana Buddha, whose pure eyes bloom like blue lotuses;
relying upon the King of Sūtras, the Mahāvairocana, I shall explain the various ritual procedures for making offerings,
so that the methods of mantras may be accomplished in their proper sequence, and one may thereby swiftly attain realization as taught therein.

If you wish to enter siddhi in this very life, do not harbor thoughts of disparagement toward the preceptor who conferred the precepts or your fellow practitioners; do not perform the conduct of a foolish child,
and do not give rise to resentment toward the honored ones.
Nothing can damage great benefit more than anger;
by the conditions of a single thought, all that has been cultivated over millions of eons is utterly consumed. Therefore, one should always diligently abandon it.
The wish-fulfilling jewel of the pure bodhicitta can fulfill all aspirations and extinguish the afflictions;
from it arise samādhi, wisdom, and mindfulness—therefore, I now diligently protect it.
Furthermore, always fully endowed with great compassion, As well as the immeasurable minds of joy and equanimity,
Having personally received the illuminating Dharma from the Honored One, One observes and practices accordingly to achieve accomplishment.
First, prostrate to the Honored One who bestows empowerment and transmits the teachings, and request permission for the mantra practice to be cultivated.
Once the wise practitioner has received the teacher’s consent, they should rely upon a suitable location according to the divisions of the earth—
such as the slopes of a wondrous mountain, a subsidiary peak, or amidst the crevices of a cliff— where lotus ponds are adorned everywhere with water lilies and blue lotuses.
Along the banks of great rivers, streams, and islands, far removed from the clamor of people and crowds,
there stand trees with spreading branches and foliage that gladden the mind, abounding in milky trees and auspicious grasses;
these are places where the Tathāgatas and their noble disciples have constantly dwelt and roamed since ancient times.
In temples, stupas, hermitages, and the dwellings of ancient seers,
one should paint great mandalas out of compassion for sentient beings. Possessing the power of pure wisdom and the capacity for endurance,
one should diligently purify and repent all transgressions born of negligence during that night.
With mind and eyes gazing clearly and with perfect clarity, I cast my five limbs upon the ground in prostration.
I take refuge in the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the ten directions; I take refuge in all those of the three times who possess the three bodies;
I take refuge in the entire Mahāyāna Dharma; I take refuge in the assembly of those who do not regress from Bodhi.
I take refuge in the true words of all vidyās; I take refuge in all secret mudrās.
With the pure karma of body, speech, and mind, I pay homage with diligent and immeasurable reverence.
Having prostrated three times and circumambulated three times while offering praise, when wishing to depart, one again prostrates and praises three times.
The mantra is called the Earth-Holding Seal (Dharādhara-mudrā).
There are four names for the hand seals: the right wisdom-hand is called vipaśyanā;
the left concentration-hand is named samādhi and is also called śamatha.
Accumulated by me through ignorance, I have committed various offenses through the actions of body,
speech, and mind; because my heart was shrouded by greed, hatred, and delusion, [I have erred] toward the Buddha, the True Dharma, and the Noble Sangha,
toward my parents, my two teachers, and spiritual friends, as well as toward immeasurable sentient beings.
Throughout the beginningless flow of birth and death, I have committed most grievous and inexhaustible sins;
now, in the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions who dwell in the present, I confess them all and vow never to commit them again.
The mantra for the purification of transgressions is as follows, accompanied by the Great Wisdom Sword Mudrā:
*Namo* to the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, To the treasury of the True Dharma of the three eternal bodies,
And to the assembly of the great mind of supreme vows and bodhicitta— I now take refuge in all of them with perfect sincerity.
The mantra for taking refuge is the Universal Seal (*viśvāmudrā*):
"I purify this body, free from all defilements, along with the bodies, speech, and minds of the three times—
more numerous than the atoms within oceans of buddha-fields— and offer them to all the Tathāgatas."
The mantra for the offering of the body is as follows, with the single-pronged mudrā:
The jewel of the supreme vow of the pure bodhicitta, I now arouse to deliver all sentient beings—
Those bodies entangled by the accumulation of birth-suffering and the like, And those bodies harmed by ignorance.
Rescuing, gathering, and providing refuge to bring about liberation, one should always benefit all sentient beings.
The mantra for generating the bodhicitta, with the mudrā of concentration, is as follows:
Within the infinite worlds of the ten directions, To the ocean-like assembly of all the Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
Through the power of various skillful means, and all the meritorious deeds and practices cultivated by the sons of the Buddha for the sake of sentient beings— I now rejoice in them all.
The Mantra of Rejoicing (*Anumodanā*) is as follows:
With palms joined in homage—also known as the *vajra-añjali*—I now entreat all Tathāgatas, the Greatly Awakened Ones who save the world:
I pray that throughout the realms of the ten directions, you will constantly let fall the rain of Dharma from great clouds.
The mantra for the exhortation is the Universal Seal (Samantamudrā):
"May all ordinary beings, in the places where they dwell, Swiftly cast off these bodies accumulated through manifold sufferings,
And attain the stainless realm, Abiding in the body of the pure Dharma-realm."
The mantra for invoking the Dharmakāya is as follows; the mudrā is the Universal Seal:
Whatever wholesome karmas I have cultivated, For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I now dedicate them all perfectly, To eliminate the suffering of birth and death and reach Bodhi.
The mantra for dedication is as follows; the seal is universal:

To cause body and mind to be thoroughly purified, Out of compassion, to rescue and protect oneself and others, One should sit comfortably according to what is appropriate, And clearly and attentively contemplate the light of the first syllable.
The ninefold wheel-enclosure is empty, circular, and white; With right mindfulness, I direct my mind toward the four immeasurables.
Entering into compassion, I universally take the six realms as my object; All sentient beings possess the Tathāgatagarbha.
Through the three kinds of vajra—body, speech, and mind— And by the power of the merit I have cultivated,
Entering together into the body of the Samantabhadra Dharma-realm,
the mantra of the Samādhi of Great Compassion is as follows:
With a heart of compassion, I take pity on all sentient beings, Who are submerged in saṃsāra and lost in false discrimination.
Arising from those afflictions and secondary afflictions, Failing to realize the principle of the equality of True Suchness (Tathatā),
And surpassing all merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— By the power of the three secrets I have cultivated,
I universally pray that all may become equal to the Treasury of Space (Gaganagañja).
The mantra of the Samādhi of Great Compassion is as follows:
With a heart of immeasurable joy pervading the four modes of birth, Inherently pure like a lotus flower,
May all that is practiced and all sentient beings Together realize the body of Avalokiteśvara.
The mantra of the Samādhi of Great Joy is as follows:
The mind of equanimity is pure, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; Free from "I" and "mine," as well as the aggregates and sense bases;
With subject and object equalized, the mind does not arise; Its nature and characteristics are fundamentally quiescent, identical to the treasury of emptiness.
The mantra for the Great Equanimity Samādhi is:

Oṃ Mahāpeyāla Svāhā. Next, one should form the Samaya-mudrā: join the palms of the Wisdom and Means hands with their fingers hollowed; extend the thumbs upright like banners. This can fulfill the accumulation of merit and wisdom.
The mantra for purifying the three paths of action is as follows: By virtue of the primary samaya, one is equal to the secret body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, it is for the sake of one’s own enjoyment, for the purpose of establishing the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala, and for the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s retinue. By reciting each of the mantras of the five places once, one can eliminate past obstructions and purify oneself; because the body is purified, external obstructions are likewise purified, such that no obstacles whatsoever may enter.
This is the Great Protection; it is the awakening by all Buddhas that fulfills one's aspirations.
Because the seal of the Dharma is not opened, one is not permitted to hear all dharmas.
If one does not perform this first, it will not be suitable for accomplishing all dharmas:
by merely forming this seal, one is able to purify the stage of the Tathāgata,
fulfill the pāramitā of the stages, and realize the path of the three dharma realms.
Next, one binds the Dharmadhātujāta mudrā, the emblem of secret wisdom.
Because it purifies body, speech, and mind, it is rotated throughout all parts of the body. Its mantra is: [Oṃ dharmadhātujāya svāhā].
By means of this second samaya, one attains a body equal to the majestic form of the Honored One within the Palace of the Dharmadhātu, sustained by the Tathāgata’s empowerment.

Furthermore, it is for the sake of bringing to fulfillment the Bodhisattvas of the Dharmatā-body; for the sake of acting as the Vairocana-ācārya; and for the sake of bestowing empowerment upon the retinue of the Lotus Family.

Form fists with both hands separately; extend the index fingers and hold them at the chest, turning them inward. Drag the tips of the two index fingers from both sides of the crown toward the center, with the backs of the fingers facing inward, gradually bringing them together at the heart and then releasing them.
In all recitations of mantras and formations of mudrās, one should be like two oxen plowing together, proceeding side by side without one preceding or following the other:
contemplating one's own body as the self-nature of the Dharmadhātu,
in order to make that [realization] firm, one contemplates oneself as Vajradhara.
Form the Vajracakra-mudrā.
The mantra of Vajrasattva is as follows: "By means of the third samaya, may my own body and the earth become like vajra, and may I be surrounded by an immeasurable host of Vajradharas."

Furthermore, for the sake of subduing and gathering sentient beings according to their respective types, for the sake of the activities of the Vajradhara disciple, and for the sake of empowering the vajra retinue—specifically, to adorn the body of Vajrasattva—the three samayas are fully explained.

By means of mantras and mudrās, one causes both body and mind to be purified; one is able to directly perceive the turning of the Dharma wheel of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the threefold following-turning, and is able to turn the unsurpassed Great Dharma Wheel throughout the great trichiliocosm:
"Contemplate this body of mine as being none other than Vajrapāṇi;
next, don the vajra armor, and one should contemplate the garment thus worn."
His entire body blazes with radiant flames.
That mantra is as follows:
The syllable RA is brilliant white, adorned with the bindu of emptiness.
Just as that bright jewel in a topknot, when placed upon the crown of the head,
causes all accumulated stains of sin to be entirely eliminated,
so that merit and wisdom are both brought to perfection.
One should add this gateway of letters: red in color, endowed with majestic radiance, and completely encircled by a wreath of flames.
To subdue all great obstructors, one should recollect the Great Protector.
No one is able to endure their brilliance.

The Buddhas, through the power of their equanimity, do not abide in quiescence but manifest great skillful means; because their majestic radiance is so fierce and intense, it is like a newborn infant who cannot bear to look upon the light of the scorching sun.
This is likewise so; none are able to endure it or dare to eclipse or seize it.
This Vidyārāja protects the practitioner with this mantra, which says:
"By the mere recollection [of me], all Vināyakas..."
The Rākṣasas of hideous form and all others shall flee and disperse.
One should awaken the Earth Deity and recite these verses while kneeling with both knees on the ground.
Holding the vajra at the heart with the hand of wisdom,
extend the five fingers of the palms and press them against the earth: *Tvaṃ yanīve*.
1. *Dharaṇīndrātmajā* (The daughter of the Earth-God). 2.
*Sarvabuddhādhyeṣaṇī* (She who requests all the Buddhas). 3. *Tāyinī* (The Savior;
she who possesses the meaning of a guide). 4. *Caryā* (Conduct).

Ākṛṣya (draw forth), naya (lead), pūraya (fulfill), vaśīkuru (bring under control), āveśaya (cause to enter), viśeṣaya (make excellent)—these three; Amogha-siddhi (accomplishment of the unobstructed), guhya-pada-pramuditā-tīrthānām (of those who have reached the joyful ground of the secret state)—these four;
Māra-bala-sainya-vidhvaṃsana (the destruction of the hosts and armies of the Māras)—five;
Śākyasiṃha-nāthasya (of the Lion of the Śākyas, the Protector)—six.

6. Savior of the World (*Jagat-trāṇa*): *tathāgato ’haṃ māra-māraya jvala kṛta-vajra-pūjita*. 7. Maṇḍala-likhana-mantra: *maṇḍala-lekhaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. 8. The mantra for the Earth Goddess (*Pṛthivī-devī*) to be recited in sequence is as follows:
Form the vajra-bind (*vajrabandha*), open the palms and press them upward; practice this twenty-one times, and likewise press them downward.
This immediately becomes the Firm Ground (*Dṛḍhābhūmi*).
The mantra for constructing the maṇḍala is: *Oṃ dṛṃ khaṃ*.

The mantra for sprinkling purification (*prokṣaṇa*) is: *Oṃ natha natha dhiti dhiti nathapariśodhani svāhā*. Regarding the ritual hand gestures (*mudrā*): place the fist of the Samādhi-hand at the side of the waist; extend the fingers of the Wisdom-hand, join the Wind and Space fingers together, and with this, perform the universal purification by sprinkling [water] on the five places of the body.
Next, the offerings of incense, flowers, food, and clothing, along with the boundary-binding:
May all Buddhas who compassionately regard sentient beings Please turn their mindful attention toward us.
I now respectfully entreat all the worthy sages, The Earth Goddess Sthāvarā and her retinue.
All Tathāgatas and their spiritual heirs, Without forsaking your compassionate vows, descend upon this place;
I receive this ground seeking accomplishment— Act as my witnesses and grant me your protection.
The mantra for Holding the Earth is as follows: Form the *samādhi-muṣṭi* (the concentration-fist) as described before;

with the wisdom hand, extend it downward to press upon the earth: *Namo samantabuddhānām | Sarvatathāgatadhiṣṭhānadhiṣṭhite | ājñāpayasi | vimale | samalaye | prākṛtipariśuddhe | svāhā.* At that time, the Bhagavān surveyed the entire *dharmadhātu* and entered the *dharmadhātukuṭī*.
By means of the Tathāgata’s Samādhi of the Arrayed Treasury of Equalized Vigor,
clouds of manifested bodies emerge from every pore, producing immeasurable Buddhas.
Because the manifest dharma-realm is adorned with inexhaustibility,
one delivers the entire realm of sentient beings without exception through this gateway of mantra practice,
thereby fulfilling one's original vow.
From the gateway of the multitude of sounds, they emit voices that accord with the various types of beings,

according to their inherent nature, karma-born conditions, accomplishments, enjoyments, retributions, manifest forms, all physical appearances, diverse languages, and the thoughts within their minds, thereby preaching the Dharma for them.
Causing all sentient beings to attain joy.
Having performed the successive empowerment, he returned to the palace within the Dharma-realm and again addressed the Lord of Secrets:
"There are seed-syllables and insignia representing the positions of the holy deities for constructing a maṇḍala."
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
I shall now expound the udāna known as the fivefold samaya:
first, the principal deity; second, the mantra; third, the secret mudrā; fourth, the samādhi; and fifth, the seed-syllable.
“The thorough student of mantras, having mastered the secret maṇḍala,
acts for the sake of disciples according to the Dharma, completely incinerating all their sins.
Their lifespan is entirely consumed by fire, causing it never to arise again.”
Once reduced to ashes, that life-span is restored.
By burning the syllable with the syllable, one is reborn through the syllable;
thus all life arises, pure, pervasive, and stainless.
By means of the twelve links of existence, one fashions that vessel.
Such is the samaya of all Tathāgatas,
the Bodhisattvas who save the world, and the assembly of the Buddha’s śrāvakas.
Even unto all the worlds, they remain equal and without contradiction.
Understanding this vow of equality, one enters the secret maṇḍala and the teachings of all dharmas, attaining mastery over all ritual circles.
My body is equal to that [of the deity], and the mantra practitioner is likewise;
because they are not distinct, it is called the *samaya*.
One should visualize the syllable RA before oneself as a garland of pure, radiant flames.
Brilliant as the radiance of the rising sun, the sound of recitation embodies the true meaning;
it can eliminate all obstacles and liberate one from the defilements of the three poisons.
All phenomena are likewise thus: first, purify your own mind-ground.
Furthermore, purify the site of the practice, completely eliminating all faults and afflictions.
Its characteristic is like space, supported as if by a vajra;
this ground is likewise so, abiding in the yoga of the deity.
Furthermore, by adding the five-syllable mantra and visualizing while in meditative equipoise (samādhi),
one becomes identical to the Honored One,
the Muni. Using it as a vajra-wheel, one empowers the lower body.
This is called the yoga seat.
Within the mass of mist, one empowers [the syllable] above one's navel;
this is called the water of great compassion.
The vermilion-red resides in the triangle, empowered at the position of the fundamental mind;
this is called the Fire of Wisdom.
The black resides in the wind-mandala, empowered at the limit of the white tuft.
This is called the power of mastery (*vaśitā-bala*).
By manifesting all forms through mental conception (*saṃjñā*) and sustaining them upon the crown of the head,
it is therefore named "Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*).
The torch of majestic power blazes fiercely, extinguishing all karmic offenses;
even those celestial Māras who act as obstacles behold the resplendent Vajra.
With the King of a Hundred Lights at the crown of the head and the syllable of non-arising placed in the heart, [one is liberated].
On the chest, visualize the syllable Virañci (Vi), Establishing the stainless eye.
Contemplate the body as identical to the Tathāgata, And further recite the verse of fulfillment:
"Establishing the receptacle world: Space and wind abide at the very bottom."
Next, one contemplates fire, water, and earth; this wheel is identical to the vajra and is named Mahendra.
It flows forth everywhere and in all directions; next, one should mindfully maintain the earth.
And [one] depicts various forms and images.
At that time, the Bhagavān, having observed the great assembly,
addressed the Lord of Secrets, saying:
Because his body was thus adorned, as he traversed through the cycle of birth and death,
amidst the great assemblies of the Tathāgatas,
the gods, nāgas, and yakṣas paid him reverence and received his instructions, which bore the banner and insignia of Bodhi.
First is the Seal of the Buddha-Samādhi: join the palms at the dharma-realm and the wheel of Dharma;
with the thumbs and ring fingers joined in homage, bend the wind-wheel (index finger) to rest against the side of the fingernail of the space-wheel (little finger).
The dharma-conch, hollow palms joined, winds churning upon the wheel of space;
the auspicious lotus of aspiration, the seal of great vajra wisdom;
the crown of the Mahā-tathāgata, the wisdom-fist concealed within the ūrṇā-kośa.
The mudrā of the yogin holding the alms-bowl has the hand of wisdom extended upward;
it is called the "Fearless Bestower," while that which hangs downward is known as the "Fulfilling Wishes" palm.
The Wisdom Fist extends the fire and water while pressing upon space;
the wise one attains the Buddha-eye by binding the wind-wheel with the cord within, and the Mind Seal extends the fire-wheel.
The navel of the Tathāgata Śuśu is formed by the previous mudrā with the wind entering the moon; this is called the Tathāgata’s waist.
Recite the mantra accordingly.
The mantra of the Great Wisdom Sword (*Mahāprajñā-khaḍga*) is as follows: *Vajra-añjali* (also known as *Namo*).
The sword is a metaphor for sharp wisdom, with the meaning of being able to sever and eliminate.
It removes the mountain peaks of evil views; just as the peaks of a great mountain are vast and disordered in great number, so too are the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Now, this mudrā can sever the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), along with innate views, the sixty-two views, and so forth. This sword is great wisdom; alternatively, it is said that when concentration and wisdom are joined in an empty mind, they can sever all afflictions and attain the stainless *dharmakāya*.

*Namo samantabuddhānām | mahākhaḍgavijaya | dharmasandarśaka-sahaja | siddhyānartiṣṭhanoka | tathāgatavimukti-nirjāta | vijayadharmajita hūṃ ||* The mantra of the Great Dharma Conch (*mahādharmaśaṅkha*) is as follows: Hold it near the mouth and blow upon it in the manner of blowing a conch, rotating it to the left and right.
Namo samanta buddhānām Āḥ. By this, one immediately fulfills all virtuous aspirations and proclaims the Great Dharma so that it may be universally heard and known.
This is the mantra of the Lotus Seat, the Seal of Quiescent Nirvāṇa:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām āḥ*. Because the Vajra-seat is seated upon this, all Buddhas are born from it.
The mudrā is named Śrīparyaṅka.
The Vajra-Indestructible Ā-born Great Wisdom Vajra-mantra of all Buddhas is the Five-Peaked Mudrā:
*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ hūṃ*. The Tathāgata-Uṣṇīṣa mantra is: "He who is identical to the bodies of all Buddhas."
Place the crown-mudrā at the crown of the head and visualize the Buddha entering within one’s body, his marks and signs complete:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ hūṃ hūṃ*, which possesses the meaning of the three liberations.
The former serves as the cause and the latter as the fruit.

The cause is the practice of the Tathāgata, and the fruit is the Buddha. The mantra for the Tathāgata’s Uṣṇīṣa is as follows: the Ācārya forms a fist with his right hand and places it upon the crown of the head while performing empowerment.

None of the celestial deities can see the mark of his crown: *Namo samanta-buddhānām gati-gana* (the immeasurable space), *ananta-spharaṇe viśuddha-dharmanirjāte dharmadhātu-je svāhā*. This is the mantra for the treasury of the ūrṇā-kośa (the hair-treasure between the brows). Placing the "wisdom-fist" at the location of the ūrṇā, its light pervades the ten directions;

it is able to fulfill all vows through the cause of pure precepts. *Namo samanta-buddhānām āḥ haṃ jaḥ*. This is the mantra for the great bowl. To perform it: take the inner corner of the *kāṣāya* and the corner used for draping over the shoulder; circling them around the elbow, bring them back into the hands so that the two corners resemble a pair of ears.
With both hands, draw [the cloth] upward to the navel; the shape formed by holding the bowl is identical to that of the Tathāgata.
This ritual, which holds the insignia of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, enables sentient beings who are not yet vessels for the Dharma to become fit vessels:

*Namo samantabuddhānām* (pronounce "Bō" with an upward tone and urgency). Because [all phenomena] are fundamentally unborn (*mūlato 'jātatvāt*), one transcends the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) and attains the true existence of the Tathāgata, namely the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas. The mantra for bestowing fearlessness is as follows: with the left hand, hold the two corners of the robe as previously described.
This mudrā can eliminate all the various fears, anxieties, and afflictions of sentient beings, causing them to be immediately pacified;
it also removes all manner of great terrors yet to come: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ svāhā, vanye rṇa rṇa paramārthe*.
*Erṇa erṇa*: "most excellent" means that one is able to overcome them. First, one is freed from the afflictions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

next, one is freed from the afflictions of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). The repetition of *peyaṃsaṇa* means "removing fear. *Svāhā* is the mantra for fulfilling wishes. Regarding the holding of the robe as before, with the palms extended outward as if offering water:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ vārāṇaye vajra-tmakāya*. (Homage to all Buddhas; O you who are the source of liberation, you whose body is of diamond nature.)

The meaning is: "I pray that all Buddhas grant me a vajra-body. This is also receiving the body of great wisdom; it is simply the fulfillment of one's aspiration. *Svāhā*. The mantra for the eyes born of compassion (*karuṇā*) is as follows: Place the earth-mudrā (thumb) over the wind-mudrā (ring finger), with the back of the hand facing upward. With the hands reversed, adorn the eyes three times. This forms the seal of the golden probe (*sauvarṇa-śalākā*) for removing the film of darkness. First apply it to the right eye, then the left.
By means of this secret expedient, one can purify the faculty of the eye and achieve the Buddha-eye, thereby attaining vision of the Tathāgata’s profound and secret realm.

With the fleshly eye, one sees all forms; with the heavenly eye, one sees the minds of all sentient beings; with the wisdom eye, one sees the realms of the faculties of all sentient beings; with the Dharma eye, one sees the true reality of all phenomena; and with the Buddha-eye, one sees the ten powers.
From the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Fascicle 57:

*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ ākāśagarbha-vajra-locana-karūṇā-maya-tathāgata-cakṣuḥ svāhā.* The mantra of the Tathāgata’s Eye is as follows: This eye arises from the Tathāgata’s faith and understanding (*adhimukti*); through the power of faith and understanding, it manifests in various forms and types—sometimes appearing as wrathful deities, sometimes as vidyādharas—possessing great power and majesty to gather and transform sentient beings.
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ he he.* "Call upon! Call upon! This is the cause for gathering [beings] and carries the meaning of *samādhi*.

The cause for becoming a Buddha is that this cause is fundamentally unarisen; being free from the characteristics of cause and effect, it purifies the cause so that the fruit is likewise purified. Mahāpāśa is the "Great Noose"; this cause, which is free from characteristics, is called Mahāpāśaprasāra-prayoga, which is like space.

The Great Rope is vast and universal, pervading all without exception. *Sattva* refers to sentient beings; *dhātu* refers to the realm of sentient beings, encompassing even the subtlest. *Mahākāruṇika*, O Compassionate One, remove delusion! *Tathāgata*, O Tathāgata, on the stage of the Tathāgata, may faith and understanding arise. *Muktati*. May it be so.
When the Buddhas were practicing the bodhisattva path, they established great vows to deliver all sentient beings.

Now, by means of these causes, they must realize the fruit; if they dwell in the bliss of liberation and do not recall their original vow, they would violate their fundamental aspiration, which is also termed delusion.
In order to eliminate this delusion, may you enter so as to ultimately and perpetually perform the Buddha’s work; svāhā! May you bind and destroy those who create obstacles and difficulties.

Born from the power of resolute faith, it can manifest various forms; through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), it delivers sentient beings. To eliminate the winds of distraction and sever the fetters, the Tathāgata’s Heart Mantra is as follows: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ jñānāgniye*. This is the wisdom of all Buddhas. [The mudrā: Do not change the previous fingers;

extend the fire-fingers (*tarjanī*) side by side and slightly bend them. This can give rise to great wisdom, benevolence, compassion, and profound, vast, and great skillful means (*upāya*). *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ jñānāgniye*. This is the wisdom of all Buddhas.
This wisdom is not obtained from another; it arises from the Buddha-mind, arises from the *uṣṇīṣa*. Svāhā. The mantra for the Tathāgata’s navel is: Amṛte, the Nectar.
“Amṛta” (Nectar) is another name for wisdom; it can eliminate the feverish afflictions of body and mind. By obtaining and consuming it, one attains a long-lived body that neither ages nor dies.
Regarding the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*), the fingers are slightly bent, etc.:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām amṛtodbhavāya amṛtāya hṛdaya-saṃtāpa-vinodanāya upavauṣaṭ svāhā*. This is the mantra of the Tathāgata’s waist. As for the mantra of the Buddha’s wondrously colored body: the hands of wisdom (*prajñā-hasta*)—earth, water, fire, and wind—as before, are all slightly bent. It is the self-nature that accomplishes noble wisdom.
The *tsaṃ* seal: join the palms with hollowed centers; bend the wind-wheels (*anāmikā*) to press down, while the earth and water wheels (*tarjanī*) are slightly curved.
The light-wheels (*madhyamā*) cross within the fire-wheels (*kaniṣṭhā*), the space-entry (*aṅguṣṭha*) disperses toward the wind and water, and the earth-wheels are joined upright.
Join the thumbs with palms hollow; place the wind-banner (index fingers) behind the fire (middle fingers).
Insert the two tongues (ring fingers) into the voids (thumbs).
At the gate of speech (little fingers), the wind and water (index and ring fingers) are rounded, aligned with the voids (thumbs) in the shape of a mouth.
The "Tusk Seal" (daṃṣṭramudrā) has the wind element entering the palms as before.
For the two wind wheels of "Discourse" (vāda), follow the previous seal; at the third joint of the side of the fire wheel, the space wheel (ākāśacakra) moves slightly.
The ten powers are like lotus petals closing; the earth and space are bent and enter the moon. The joints within the palms are joined together.
For the foundations of mindfulness, the wind-finger pinches the space as in the previous seal.
Awakening opens the round seal of the *kavaca*; earth, water, and space enter the palm.
Samantabhadra’s wish-fulfilling jewel: the lotus closes, wind adds fire; the upper joint takes the form of a treasure.
Maitreya’s mudrā is as before, with the wind and fire fingers (the index and middle fingers) bent down;
from the space [between them], he offers a wondrous *kundikā* (water flask).
The mantra of the Tathāgatagarbha is for the purpose of removing the two veils of defilement and realizing the Buddha’s pure body:

*Namo sarvatathāgatebhyaḥ*. This removes the defilements of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). *Svāhā*. This removes the defilements of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). The Universal Radiance Mantra (*Samantaprabhā*) is also called the Perfect Halo (*Parimaṇḍala-prabhā*). It is as follows: *Namo samantabuddhānām*. *Jvala-mālini*. "Mālā" means a garland;

because it forms a continuous circle of flames like a wreath, it is called the Tathāgata’s Perfect Halo. *Tathāgata-locane*. This is the clear light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. *Svāhā*. The Tathāgata Armor Mantra (*Tathāgata-kavaca*) is as follows: Join the palms of concentration and wisdom with the hollows facing each other. Hold the wind-finger (ring finger) at the side of the fire-wheel (middle finger). The space-finger (thumb) should be separated from the fire-finger (middle finger) by about the size of a barley grain.
Just as a Bodhisattva in his final birth must don this armor of unsurpassed enlightenment, sit upon the Vajra-seat, subdue all demonic armies, and achieve perfect awakening.
The mantra practitioner must don this armor to perform the Buddha-activities:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ pracaṇḍavajra-jvala-karaviśphura vya hūṃ*. The mantra of the Tathāgata’s tongue-mark is as follows: "One attains the tongue of the Tathāgata; the Dharma-sound pervades the ten directions; one always speaks according to reality, being neither deceptive, nor delusive, nor inconsistent; because it is true, it abides eternally."

*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgatajihvā-satyadharma-pratiṣṭhita-satyadharmatā svāhā.* The mantra of the Tathāgata’s speech is as follows: it signifies that this speech arises from the Tathāgata’s skillful wisdom through immeasurable gateways.
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgata-mahā-vāk-viśva-jñāna-mahodara svāhā.* The mantra of the Tathāgata’s fangs is as follows:

*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgatāgata-ghoṣeśvara-svara-svaramadhyasvarakrama-saṃprabhoga-deya sarvatathāgata-viṣaya-sambhava svāhā.* The mantra for the eloquence of the Tathāgatas is as follows: By means of this mudrā, one dwells among the assembly without fear; when preaching the True Dharma for others, even a single word contains infinite meanings, and one’s eloquence shall be inexhaustible.

*Namo samantabuddhānām*. O you who possess inconceivable power (*acintyānubhava*), you who are marvelous and extraordinary (*vicitrarūpa*), you who are the manifestation of speech (*vāk-saṃdhi*), you who reach everywhere (*samanta-prāpta*); the Buddha, with a single voice, expounds the Dharma and so forth (*prabhāsvara*). *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Tathāgata’s Ten Powers (*daśabala*) is as follows: By means of this seal of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*), one is able to uphold the constituent parts of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.

*Namo samantabuddhānām*. O you whose body is the ten powers (*daśabala-kāya*), you who hold the *īśvara*, *hūṃ*, *triṇi*, *svāhā*. The mantra of the Tathāgata’s Foundations of Mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is as follows:

*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgatasamṛddhisatvahitavibudhagaganasamasvāhā.* The mantra for awakening to the equality of all phenomena is as follows: *Namo samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgatasamṛddhisatvahitavibudhagaganasamasvāhā.* *Homage to all Buddhas! To the Tathāgata, the perfection of the assembly, the one who brings about the welfare of sentient beings, the one who arises, the one whose nature is like space, the peerless one—svāhā!* The mantra for the realization of the equality of all dharmas is: *Namo samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgatasamṛddhisatvahitavibudhagaganasamasvāhā.* *Homage to all Buddhas! To the Tathāgata, the prosperity of the assembly, the benefit of sentient beings, the arising, the one equal to space, the incomparable one—svāhā!* The mantra for the true awakening to the equality of all phenomena is: *Namo samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgatasamṛddhisatvahitavibudhagaganasamasvāhā.* *Homage to all Buddhas! To the Tathāgata, the perfect accomplishment, the thought of sentient beings, the welfare of beings, the arising, the one whose nature is space, the unequaled one—svāhā!*

*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ sarvadharmasamatāprabhāvitathāgatānugata-svāhā.* Above, this is the mantra of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, from the Assembly of the Tathāgata’s Body. This Bodhisattva’s three karmas are universally virtuous and excellent, and he is revered and praised by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. *Note on transliteration:* *Namo samantabuddhānāṃ sarvadharmasamatāprabhāvitathāgatānugata-svāhā* (曩莫三曼多沒馱喃薩嚩達麼一切法三麼多平等鉢囉二合鉢多二合，至也得也，一切平等怛他引蘖多如來弩蘖多隨同佛如是開悟娑嚩二合賀) *Note on the title:* *Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s Wish-Fulfilling Jewel Mantra* (普賢菩薩如意珠真言) *Note on the description:* "This Bodhisattva’s three karmas are universally virtuous and excellent, and he is revered and praised by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas" (此菩薩所有三業普遍賢善，諸佛菩薩之所敬歎也)

*Namo samantabuddhānām* (Homage to all Buddhas). *Samanta* means "all-pervading" or "reaching everywhere"; *anugata* means "following" or "entering"; *vimala* means "stainless," referring to being free from the defilements of obstruction; *dharma* means "Dharma"; *niḥsṛta* means "arisen from. Thus, it is said that he is stainless and arises from the Dharma. *Mahā mahā* is repeated for emphasis, meaning "Great, Great One," like a god among gods.
The various bodhisattvas make offerings to the Buddha, and the Buddha in turn makes offerings to Samantabhadra; the body of the bodhisattva is equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Among the great offerings of the God of Gods, he makes offerings with *svāhā*. From this, the myriad practices for awakening arise, and all vows are fulfilled; therefore, it is called a "jewel. The mantra of Maitreya Bodhisattva is as follows: Abiding in the samādhi that universally generates great compassion. The mudrā is the same as that of the stūpas of all Buddhas.

*Namo samantabuddhānām*. *Ati-r-dan-ku-yun* means Ajita; its meaning is "unsurpassed. Because he has attained victory (*jaya*) over all afflictions of attachment and views as well as those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), he is "victorious among the unsurpassed" (*ajite jita*). *Sarvasattvānām*: all sentient beings. *Śaya* refers to their nature, the nature of the mind (*cittatā*), meaning the knowledge of the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations (*indriya-gotra-śaya*) cultivated in previous lives. *Svāhā*. At that time, the Buddha dwelt in the *Amṛta-janma-samādhi* and spoke this vidyā-mantra of the consort of unimpeded power throughout the three times. The *mūrdha-mudrā* (crown seal) is used here in the same manner as the *Ākāśākṣī* (Space-Eye) consort in the second fascicle. *Namo samantabuddhānām. Atirdankuyun ajite jaye sarvasattvānām śaya svāhā.* *The mudrā for this is the crown seal, which is employed identically to the Space-Eye consort [as described] in the second fascicle.*

*Tadyathā | gagaṇasame | apratisame | sarvatathāgatamātṛnugate | gagaṇasame | varadākṣaṇi | svāhā.* Recite this mantra of the Vidyārājñī of Unassailable Power eight times while forming the Brahmā-hand mudrā. Then, arising from the preceding samādhi, enter once more into the *Anantavijaya-samādhi*:
"Purifying the Buddha-fields and serving all Tathāgatas, one clearly contemplates the ocean of fragrant waters."

The mantra of the Great Ocean is as follows: Interlace the two seals with their fingers crossed; extend the two thumbs (the *ākāśa* fingers) and rotate them to the right—this is the seal of the ocean water.

Following the previous seal, press the right *vāyu* finger-nail against the surface of the left *vāyu* finger, holding it steady and motionless—this is the seal of the eight meritorious qualities (*aṣṭaguṇa*) of water.
*Oṃ vimalanātha hūṃ*. The Vajrapāṇi Flower Seal of the Five Wisdoms within is as follows:
Vajradhara-paṇi; this great king of mantras and its mudrā are transmitted orally. With the sublime Lotus King, one sustains the Flower Treasury World (Puṣpasaṃbhava-dhātu).
The original perfect enlightenment and so forth, the arrayed maṇḍala,
the secret within secrets, the womb of great compassion from which all arises,
as well as the immeasurable mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas.
Listen as I describe in sequence all the images therein:
Surrounded on all four sides, with a single gate and passageways,
Adorned everywhere with vajra seals, and in the center, the Karma-vajra.
Upon it is a great lotus, with a wondrous-colored vajra stem;
it has eight petals complete with filaments and anthers, naturally adorned with various jewels,
fully blossomed and containing fruit.
Adorned with the point of great emptiness, the syllable from which the twelve links arise,
it stands universally upon a flower pedestal, constantly emitting immeasurable light and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of lotuses.
The lion throne of the Great Awakened One, adorned with the finest of jewels,
is situated within a vast palace.
It is everywhere graced with banners and canopies, and interlaced with strings of pearls and other ornaments.
Exquisite jewel robes hang suspended, surrounded by clouds of fragrant flowers and clouds of various jewels;
a rain of diverse blossoms falls everywhere,
scattering profusely to adorn the ground, while harmonious and enchanting sounds resound.
And various musical instruments were played;
the auspicious vase and the argha-offering vessel were present, while the king of jewel-trees blossomed,
illuminated by mani-lamps.
The consorts of the Sovereign, the Buddha’s perfections and the like,
are the exquisite flowers of the adornment of enlightenment; through skillful means they perform various arts,
chanting the sounds of the sublime Dharma as offerings to all Tathāgatas.
By the power of my merit, by the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment,
and by the power of the Dharma-realm, I abide in universal offering and universal sealing,
binding the seal of the Great Wheel Maṇḍala.

Next, regarding the paths of the various realms of form (*rūpadhātu*): the syllable *raṃ* is white, the banner of *laṃ* is red, the flower of *kaṃ* is yellow, the syllable *maṃ* is blue, and the sound-realm path of *miha* is black. One should contemplate the seed-syllables of the deities within the womb of the two seals of the Great Wisdom Vajra, arranging each one clearly and distinctly. First, one visualizes a circular light, a pure moon disc of universal radiance, with the syllable *aḥ* placed in its center.
Next, one should transform the syllable A into the Muni Mahāvairocana;
pure and free from all defilements, his wondrous form transcends the three realms.
His body is adorned with garments of fine gauze and silk, and a jeweled crown sits upon his dark-blue hanging hair.
In the state of tranquil samādhi, A radiant blaze surpasses all lightning;
Just as within a pure mirror, The profound depths reveal the true countenance,
Manifesting expressions of joy and anger, And assuming forms according to one's aspirations.
The body is in union with meditative absorption, the mind is lucid and undisturbed;
the essence of the pure dharmas is signless, fulfilling vows to save all sentient beings,
surrounded by a retinue within the eight maṇḍalas.
Next, the seal of Samantabhadra in the east;
Avalokiteśvara in the north, with Vajrapāṇi placed in the south;
in the direction of Nirṛti is the messenger of Akṣobhya Tathāgata; and in the direction of wind is Trailokyavijaya.
The Four Great Protectors of the four directions:
in the third [direction] is Mañjuśrī; in the south is Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin;
in the victorious direction is Kṣitigarbha; and in the nāga direction is Ākāśagarbha.
The retinue of Susiddhi and the majestic world-protecting devas are distributed in succession;
next, one should hold the incense burner.
The mantra for purification is as follows:
The Great Vidyārāja Acala removes defilements and renders them pure;
he expels obstacles to make [the site] radiant, and provides protection for the body and the boundary.
That mantra is as follows: The Tathāgata, in order to pacify all obstacles, abiding in the *Agnijvāla-samādhi*, spoke this mantra for destroying great hindrances.

It means that from the first generation of the bodhicitta, the practitioner shall guard and increase it until the final attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood, never falling back nor descending into the non-path of *ajñāna*.
Next, with the mudrā and mantra, one invokes the assembly of sages;
as taught by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they arrive in accordance with their original vows.
Forming fists within with the concentration and wisdom [mudrās], the wisdom-wind is bent like a hook.
When summoned, they arrive at the time of the consecration; by means of this hook-seal (*ākarṣaṇa-mudrā*), the practitioner is led through the entrance.

The mantra says: "This hook-seal is able to summon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions to assemble at the site of practice (*maṇḍala*). If it can fulfill the stages of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), how much more so would those of the eight classes of beings who have not yet given rise to a wholesome mind not come here?"
It is able to summon the great ocean of merit of all Buddhas and completely fulfill the merits of all Tathāgatas.
It universally summons all sentient beings and causes them also to attain this path:
next, the samaya is revealed—swiftly fulfilling the unsurpassed vows.
In order to cause the original mantra-lord and all the vidyās to rejoice,
next grasp the vajra, draw it back, and cast it forth while shaking the golden bell;
having performed the empowerment according to the ritual rules for the offered argha water, [proceed].
To those who honor all the Sugatas, one should bathe their stainless bodies;
first the right knee, then the left, offering three times up to the forehead.
Next, one should purify all those born from the mouth of the Buddha.
Empower the Immovable Honored One twenty-five times with the hand gestures of *padma-saṃpuṭa*, *vāyu-vartana*, and *agni-veṣṭita*;
hold the *ākāśa* at the lower joint of the *vāyu*. The mantra is: *Namo samantabuddhānām ākāśasamāsamasama svāhā.* Next, the mantra for the Flower Seat is:

*Ākarṣaya acala...* The verse for the protection of the Immovable One is: *May the ocean of pure jewel-water, its floor spread with golden sand and filled with the eight virtues, bathe all the sages so they are stainless. This Great Compassionate Womb and Ocean of Great Wisdom can wash away all defilements and realize the Dharmakāya.*
The letter Kha with the great bindu of space is placed upon the crown;
turning into a sattva, the vajra seed-heart pervades all limbs.
All phenomena are beyond verbal expression.
By possessing the seal and mantra, one is identical to Vajradhara.
That mantra is five-pronged and three-pronged:
*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ*. [This] completely covers the body with armor.
Next, one should single-mindedly perform the seal for subduing all māras,
which is in accord with the true speech.
Extending the wind-wheel (the index finger) from the wisdom-fist and placing it at the limit of the white tuft [between the brows], one assumes the form of Bhṛkuṭī.
Because one has just bound this dharma, one should visualize that the entire ground is filled with the blazing light of vajras;
it is capable of eliminating the extremely fierce and powerful armies of immeasurable celestial Māras, as well as all other obstructors.
They will certainly all retreat and disperse. With the left fist placed at the waist, the mantra for terrifying Māra is as follows:

with a face like that of a wrathful deity and the mind abiding in a single object, one can manifest the majestic and powerful force of the Tathāgata and fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings.
Under the Bodhi tree, the Tathāgata subdued all māras by means of this seal:
next, employing the Unbearable [Seal], one binds the protection with the secret mudrā and mantra;
spreading the water-wheel of the treasury-seal, one rotates it toward the ten directions.
This is called binding the great boundary,
which causes all things to abide firmly; therefore, it can universally protect all matters of the three times,
its majestic power being such that none can behold it.

The mantra of the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is as follows: from the initial generation of the mind of great enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) until the attainment of Buddhahood, one shall not allow it to be interrupted or to regress from enlightenment;
this is the meaning of the "Great Boundary. *Namo samantabuddhānām* (Homage to all Buddhas).

*Sarvatrānugate* (Pervading everywhere)—meaning that one must universally bind [the boundary] throughout the ten directions. *Bodhyākrama* (The progression toward enlightenment). *Mahāsamaya* (The great samaya). *Nirjāte* (O you who have arisen [from the samaya]). *Smaraṇi* (O mindful one). *Aparājitā* (O unconquerable one). [This concludes the mantra.]
It is also said: *Asaṅgāvināśa dhakadhaka*. By the majestic light, through that majestic light, the realm is formed.

*Vajra vajra*, go everywhere to the ten directions and bind the boundary. *Bandha bandha*, bind the *nairṛtya* [direction]. *Nityaṃ śāntāḥ sarvatathāgatāḥ*, all Tathāgatas; *nirjita*, conquered; *prāvāra*, that which is realized; *dharma-labdha*, obtained; *devi-īrye*, O Goddess of Irresistible Power; *mantra-nāthe*, O Sovereign of Mantras; *gavati*, O World-Honored One; *vikuri*, remover; it removes defilement.
*Vikurva*, as in the previous phrase, it removes the defilement of marks (*nimitta*).
The latter phrase removes the defilement of conceptual characteristics. *Śubhabījarūpaliṅge svāhā*. Second, the brief explanation of the mantra: "I take refuge in all noble and ordinary beings;
do not transgress this boundary."

If one intentionally transgresses as before, one violates the samaya and will certainly find no peace; the assembly of noble ones will impose punishment because one has overstepped the sacred word and vow:
The four great guardians of the four directions, Who destroy all fears with fearlessness, The guardians who are difficult to subdue, And the all-pervading guardians who cannot be endured.
The great boundary (mahāmaṇḍala) intersects within the fire; the two wind-wheels (vāyumaṇḍala) are spread out and relaxed.
One contemplates the high peak of the Dharma-banner (dharmadhvaja), feeling compassion for all beings without exception.
Upon the lotus pedestal in the direction of Śakra, the syllable *vaṃ* transforms through the turning of its light.
The Protector Against Fearful Bonds: golden-hued, clad in exquisite white robes, with a face manifesting slight wrath, holding a *daṇḍa* in hand;
located in the direction of the Yakṣas, marked by the letter *Ba*, he destroys all bonds of fear.
Clad in pure white garments, holding a khaṭvāṅga in hand;
in the direction of the nāgas, one contemplates the syllable *sa*, which transforms into Durjayā.
Her color is like that of the aśoka flower, wearing red robes and manifesting a smile.
He gazes upon the assembled multitude.
Yāmya then utters the syllable *haṃ* and forms the "Invincible" (*Ajita*) seal of protection;
he is black in color, wearing dark robes, with the *Vikrumila* script [inscribed] upon him, and his head is crowned with a topknot of hair.
Illuminating the realms of sentient beings, holding the *daṇḍa* mudrā,
together with all their retinues, they all sit upon white lotus flowers.
The mantras and secret mudrās have already been revealed as before.
The two guardians of each gate, the mudrā of the Samādhi of Inability,
the spreading of the wings and the opening of the wheel, the Wisdom Fist with the wind extended from the heart,
like the posture of mutual emulation, and the raising of the Wisdom Fists facing one another.
The posture is like the gesture of striking with the right fist.

The two guardians, red and white in color, assume extremely wrathful forms. Their mantra is as follows: Because these two guardians are fierce and blazing, none dare look upon them, who are like hundreds of thousands of suns; they always remain at the inner gate of the Tathāgata to carry out his commands, and no māras can disturb or confuse them.

*Namo samantavajrāṇāṃ nṛtyarṣe*—this is the name; it means "one who cannot be looked upon" or "one who transcends," and thus refers to the one who is difficult to subdue. *Mahāroṣaṇa* means "Great Wrathful One. *Kha* is the seed syllable. *Narya* means "to eat," referring to the devouring of all afflictions (*sarvakleśa*). *Svāhā stathāgata* means "all Tathāgatas, please grant your command. *Kuru* means "to act," signifying that they cause the Tathāgatas' commands to be carried out. *Svāhā*. The mantra for facing [the opponent] and protecting oneself is as follows: It is named because one faces the Invincible One (*Durjayā*) while flanking the gate. Its color is according to what was stated previously.

*Namo samantavajrāṇām*. *He* (the name) *abhayamukha*, facing [all beings]. *Mahā-pracaṇḍa*, the great and most fierce one, violent and evil. *Khāda-sarva-kuśalajāta*, eat all that is born of virtue; devour! *Krodha*, O wrathful one! *Tvarita-samaya*, quickly [fulfill] the former vow. *Smara*, remember! Having previously made a vow before all Tathāgatas, [you who] consume all afflictions.

Why do you not now remember your original vow and perform it with haste? Svāhā. This is the mantra for the fragrant unguent (*vilepana*). Prior to this offering, water is further presented; this is set forth in the *Krama* (Succession) and its commentary.
There are four traditions regarding the offering of food: for the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and Devas. The mantra for the *arcanā* (incense) is:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vicitraśuddha-gandhodaka svāhā*. For the flower garland (*mālā*), the mantra is: [With hands] in the *añjali-mudrā*, place the palms at the forehead; rotate to the right throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*; manifesting the King of All Flowers, may all ten thousand virtues be perfectly fulfilled. *Svāhā*.

*Namo samantabuddhānām*, *mahāmaitrīcitta*, *triyā*, *mahākāruṇika viśodhaya svāhā*. This is the mantra for burning incense. The earth, water, and fire elements are turned away from one another; the two wind elements join their sides together; the space element presses against the side of the wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*); the upper joints of the four wheels of water and fire are opened; it rotates before the forehead like clouds of incense:
*Namo samantabuddhānām*, *dharmadhātugate*, *jñānagarbhe*, *anugate*, *svāhā*. This is the mantra for food and drink. [The hands] are joined in secret.
The food of Dharma-joy and the rapture of dhyāna can open the gate of ambrosia; constantly offering exquisite gifts to the Buddhas, one reaches down to spirits and ghosts, and all are reached.
By bestowing food and drink upon the field of merit, one ensures abundance and sufficiency in every lifetime:

*Namo samantabuddhānām*, *arara* (the sound that is unpleasant to hear), *asubhaśabda* (unwholesome sound), *karara* (stopping the aforementioned unwholesome sound)—this has the meaning of tranquility and stillness.
Taking the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna as food, *malina* (upper *na-da-na-mi*). This is the sacrificial food of the West; *malina-de*, having received my offering, return!

My wondrous food, *mahā-malasa*, vast, abundant, and beautiful, *svāhā*. The mantra for the lamp-light is: *Namo samantabuddhānām | tadyathā | gata-gata-ratna-jvala-spharaṇi sarvāvabhāsana ākāśagaganodariye apramāṇe ākāśasamavasaraṇe svāhā*. The mantra for the universal offering of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha is:
*Vairocana-pada*, and the place where the practitioner resides.
The assembly of beings as numerous as the atoms of the oceans of lands, surrounded by their own retinues,
then with pure and elegant voices praised the ocean of the Buddha’s merits—
the essence of the Dharma-body and the Dharma-realm.
With a pure and elegant voice, one should sing and praise the ocean of merits of all Buddhas as follows:

*Sarvavyāpī vibhogakriyā-sugata-jñānādhipate nirmāṇa-mahārala-trailokya-mahārāja namo'stu te.* I prostrate to you, the All-Pervading One, whose activity is the manifestation of the Sugatas, the Sovereign of Wisdom, the Great Jewel of Emanation, the Great King of the Three Realms. Homage be to you! I pay homage to the Sambhogakāya, the fulfillment of enlightenment. It is praised thus:

Ānanda-ma-pi-ta-sa-gu-na-ja-lam | Namo samāsajña-su-gata-tra-kara-tama-maha-mahā-nande maha-maha-hrī-ta | Maha-maha-ārya maha-maha-atmanām || The Praise of the Vajra Response Body (Vajra-sambhoga-kāya) says:
