Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-vikurvita-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra-padma-garbha-bodhidhvaja-cihna-sāmānya-mantrakośa.
From the *Mahāsiddhi-yoga-parivarta*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Faquan of Qinglong Monastery: At that time, the Bhagavān addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"There is a profound and secret dharma-gate that pervades all places."
For one who dwells in this gateway of syllables, their activities will be swiftly accomplished.
With a jeweled crown and the five-pronged hand-gesture raised, they should distribute the wheels upon their body:
at the brow, throat, heart, and navel, from the syllable *A* to *Sva-hā*.
Turning to the right in succession, the initial practice culminates in the perfection of the fruit and quiescence.
In all places of skillful means, outside the body, they appear like blazing flames;
these twelve syllables, beginning with *I*, are distributed externally.
Namo samantabuddhānām | A namo samantabuddhānām | Sa namo samantavajrāṇām | Va ka kha ga gha ṅa | Ca cha ja jha ña | Ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa | Ta tha da dha na | Pa pha ba bha ma | Ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ||
Hekṣe (pronounced with an upward tone on the first syllable),
Namo samantabuddhānām, Ā Namo samantabuddhānām,
Sva Namo samantavajrāṇāṃ Va Kha Ga Gha Ca Cha Ja Jha Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha.
TATHĀNĀTHAPRAMABHAYARĀVASAŚAHAKṢE, NAMO SAMANTABUDDHĀNĀM ĀḤ,
NAMO SAMANTABUDDHĀNĀM SAṂ, NAMO SAMANTAVAJRĀṆĀṂ BAṂ KAṂ KHAṂ.
Yan-jian-zhan-chan-ran-zhan-yan-nan-zhan-dan-tan-nan-dan-wei-shi-mie-fen-yam-lam-wan-shan-shan-san-han-ji-shan (the latter two syllables pronounced as a compound), all of which are labial sounds;
they are pronounced with the same original tone as the first rotation: *namo samantabuddhānām oṃ namo samantabuddhānām*.
Namo samantavajrāṇām | Va-jra-ya-kṣa-ja-śa-ca-cha-ta-ṭa-ḍa-dha-na-pa-bha-ma-ya-ra-la-va-śa-ṣa-sa-ha-kṣa-i-e-o-u-ri-ri.
The mantra of the samādhi-phrase of the obscured, pervasive, and profound bodhicitta is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ moadi āyaṅkṣaṇa maṃ svāhā*. The mantra for generating wisdom through the practice of bodhicitta is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ carye āyaṅkṣaṇa maṃ svāhā*. The mantra for fulfilling the requirements for attaining bodhi is:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ samādhy-āñjananāmnā svāhā.* The mantra for peaceful nirvāṇa is:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ jvalanākṣaye nāmo svāhā.* "O Lord of Secrets!"
This gateway of letters is sustained by the spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgatas.
As I now survey all the Buddha-fields universally, there is none in which this Dharma-gate, which pervades all places, is not proclaimed by those Tathāgatas.

Those who practice as bodhisattvas through the gateway of mantras should diligently study and train in this dharma-gate. By applying the initial, middle, and final syllables to *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, and *ta-pa*, and by entering into them through the categories of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they will naturally attain the practice of the bodhicitta and achieve perfect enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma just like the World-Honored One Mahāvairocana.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from the samādhi of equanimity and addressed the Lord of Secrets,
saying: "Good son,
listen attentively."
The inner maṇḍala is that very ground of the body, which is the self-nature of the dharmadhātu; it is empowered by the empowerment of mantras and secret mudrās, because its intrinsic nature is pure.
Because it is sustained by Karma-vajra, all defilements and faults—such as those of self, person, sentient being, and life-span—are purified and removed.

The square maṇḍala has four gates facing west, with thorough and circular boundary paths; within, there appears a great eight-petaled lotus king born of the mind, with upraised stalks and spread filaments, brilliantly colored and exquisitely beautiful.

Among them, the Tathāgata’s body, the most preeminent in all worlds, transcends the stages of body, speech, and mind to reach the stage of mind, thereby attaining the fruit of supreme and delightful fulfillment.
Upon the eight petals are the Tathāgatas Ratnaketu, Saṃkusumitarājendra, Amitāyus, and Dundubhisvara, as well as the Honored Ones Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Maitreya.
Within all the filaments, the Mothers of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—the Six Pāramitās—adorn themselves with their retinues of samādhis.
Below these are arrayed the various vidyādharas and wrathful deities; with the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets, serving as its stem, it stands upon the inexhaustible great ocean.
Innumerable devas dwelling on the earth surround him.

At that time, in order to fulfill the samaya, the practitioner should offer all manner of mentally conjured incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, and various delicacies, presenting them all as offerings.
The Udana says: The mantrin is truly sincere;
he draws the maṇḍala, takes his own body as the Great Self, and purifies all defilements with the syllable RAṂ.
Abiding in the yoga posture, one should call to mind all the Tathāgatas;
they bestow upon the disciples' heads the letter A, the great bindu of emptiness.
The wise one transmits the wondrous flower, causing it to be scattered over one's own body.
To explain what is seen internally, it is the place where practitioners take refuge.
Because this is the supreme maṇḍala, one should bestow the samaya.
The maṇḍala has three layers: within the golden wheel, the second and third positions are the syllable Aḥ; the third layer is yellowish-white, serving as the skillful means for all places.

At that time, Vajrapāṇi ascended into the state of the equality of the dharmas of the body, speech, and mind of the World-Honored One Mahāvairocana; mindful of future sentient beings, and in order to sever all doubts, he spoke this Great King of Mantras, abiding in the contemplation of the equality of the Dharmadhātu:

*Namo samantabuddhānām* (Homage to all Buddhas). *Asaṃbhadha* (O Unfailing One), *ananta-dharmadhātu-gatānām* (of those who have transcended the infinite realm of phenomena). *Sarvatha* (In every way), *aṃ khaṃ kaṃ vaṃ saḥ haṃ saḥ haṃ* (The seed-syllables of the earth, space, wind, fire, and water wheels). *Hūṃ raṃ vaṃ* (These are the mantras for this body). *Ha ra haṃ haḥ* (This is the mantra for speech). *Saḥ haṃ haḥ* (The mantra for the mind). At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana again surveyed the great assembly and addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets, saying: "O Son of the Buddha!"

There are eight secret mudrās that are most secret; they share the majestic power of the rank of the noble deities and serve as the insignia of the Way of Truth (Mantranaya). One should diagram their maṇḍalas in accordance with the corresponding deities.

Bodhisattvas who practice the bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras according to the scriptural teachings should understand that their own bodies abide as the form of the deity, firm and immovable.
Having known the deity, one attains siddhi by abiding as the deity.
What are the eight mudrās?
"The jewel-banner is the color of the sun’s radiance, triangular and endowed with light."
The wind of the lotus petals disperses the ground, Causing the pure golden [lotus] to bloom;
The syllable *bā* is the light of Vajra, With the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) bent within space.
Amitābha is of true golden color, Surrounded by the moon-disk and the *pātala* flower.
The blossoming, wondrous lotus;
the Drum-Sound Maṇḍala, encircled by a half-moon and a bindu, with the two earths entering the full moon.
The Samantabhadra Maṇḍala, surrounded by a full moon and vajras.
The Lotus [Bodhisattva] holds two upright *śūnyatā* (empty) fingers.

Avalokiteśvara is the color of crystal; his rainbow-colored *vajra*-banner is formed by bending the fire-wheel (*anāmikā*) as before into a hook-like shape with the fingers turned away from each other.
Mañjuśrī is the color of saffron; surrounded by a variegated halo of space, he holds a blooming blue lotus with a wheel of fire at its center.
Maitreya is golden in color; the space around him is marked with blue, and his vajra-palms are rotated so that their centers touch.
The mantra for the Birth of Great Majestic Power (Mahātejas) spoken by Ratnaketu Buddha is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ raṃ svāhā*. The mantra of the Indestructible Vajra (Vajrābhedyā) spoken by Saṃkusumita Buddha is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vaṃ vaḥ svāhā*. The mantra of the Lotus Treasury (Padmagarbha) spoken by Amitābha Buddha is: *Amitābha*.
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ saḥ svāhā.* The mantra for the adornment of all virtues, the Drum-Sound (*Duṇḍubhisvara*), is:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ haṃ hoḥ svāhā.* The mantra for the arising of all limbs, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, is:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ aṃ aḥ svāhā.* The World-Honored One’s dhāraṇī is:

Namo samanta-buddhānām | Buddha-dharani | Samṛti-mala-dhānakari | Dhara dhara dhāraya dhāraya svāhā | Bhagavati | Akāravati samaye svāhā. The mantra for the Dharma-abiding of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is as follows;
according to some texts, it is "Blue Lotus Opening Fire-Wind": Namo samanta-buddhānām | Ave naviṇe svāhā. [Secret Seal.]

First, the eight lion thrones and flower seals are positioned slightly closer together. Upon them are blue lotuses from which fire and wind emanate; atop these are placed the *brahmakapāla* (Brahma-script) seals. Above the seals, the mantra of the Lotus Swift Maitreya Bodhisattva is as follows:

*Namo samantabuddhānām | Mahāyogayoginī | Yogīśvarī | Khañjarīṭī | Svāhā.* At that time, the World-Honored One again dwelt in the unimpeded power of the three times, relying upon the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment and the Samādhi of the Adorned Pure Treasury.

Immediately, the World-Honored One emerged from samāpatti, manifesting inexhaustible realms and inexhaustible verbal expressions. Relying on the power of the Dharma-realm, the peerless power, and the conviction of the Perfectly Enlightened One, he caused a single voice to flow forth from four locations, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, equal to space, reaching everywhere without exception.
The mantra is as follows; the Root Seal (mūla-mudrā) is to be secretly transmitted by the master:

*Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo viśvamukhebhyaḥ sarvathā ā ā aṃ aḥ*. Immediately, one abides in the Samādhi of the Arising of Wisdom (*jñānotpatti-samādhi*) and recites the mantra for the Universal Illumination of Hundred Lights (*śata-prabhā-spharaṇa*), which produces various skillful wisdoms: With the vajra-palms extended upward from the arms, shaking them from time to time:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām aṃ*. To spread the King of Hundred Lights, the syllable *aṃ* is placed in the center, followed by the twelve [vowels] arranged in a circle, beginning with *i* and ending with *u-au*.

The second [set] consists of twenty-five syllables beginning with *ka*; the third wheel consists of twenty-five beginning with *kha*; the fourth consists of twenty-five beginning with *ga*; and the fifth consists of twenty-five beginning with *gha*.
Rotate the cloth to the right, joining the edges together, and perform the empowerment thirty-seven times.
"Lord of Secrets! This is called the Tathāgata’s Secret Seal.

It is the most supreme secret and should not be bestowed upon others indiscriminately, except for those who have received initiation, whose nature is gentle and compliant, who are diligent and steadfast, who have made sublime vows, who revere their teachers, who are mindful of their kindness and virtue, who are pure both internally and externally, and who seek the Dharma even at the cost of their own lives."
"Furthermore, O Lord of Secrets!
Just as the pure full moon, within which the color of a conch shell appears,
so too do all the Buddhas' triangles reside within the white lotus."
The seed-syllable of emptiness serves as its emblem, encircled by the vajra seal.
From that King of Mantras, light radiates in all directions;
seated beneath the Bodhi tree, the Buddha held this [mantra] to subdue the four Māras.
Named the Seal of Universal Wisdom, he is able to possess manifold merits and give birth to the kings of all samādhis— Gayākāśyapa,
Nadīkāśyapa, and Uruvilvākāśyapa.
The Teacher, Mother of all Buddhas, radiant with the color of pure gold,
clad in garments of white silk, shines everywhere like the light of the sun,
dwelling in meditative absorption within samādhi.
Furthermore, there are the seventy million Buddha-mothers and bodhisattvas;
the Great Heroic Bodhisattvas, Mahāsukha-Amoghasiddhi,
and the Jewel of Vajrasamādhi— all these bodhisattvas who save the world.
The seal of the Great Virtuous Holy Honored One is named "Fulfiller of All Wishes";
it is a cintāmaṇi jewel resting upon a white lotus.
The heart-mantra of all Buddhas, which universally seals, is as follows:

Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Aṃ sarvabuddhabodhisattvahṛdayaṃ jaye svāhā | Hṛdaya-veśani jaya namaḥ | Sarvavinaye svāhā. The mantra of the consort Ākāśalocanā is: Nama ākāśalocana. As for the seal of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa:

*Namo samantabuddhānām.* *Ākāśavara-lokākṣa-samaye ākāśa-gamy-e.* *Sarvatrābhyudgata-apratihata-asara-abhedya-sambhava-prabhāsa-namaskṛta-amoghe svāhā.* The mantra of all Bodhisattvas is the Universal Seal (*Sarvamudrā*):
“O Avalokiteśvara of the North, Secret Maṇḍala,
Son of the Buddha, listen with a single mind!”
Within the auspicious conch, a pāṇḍuraka lotus is born;
its petals unfold, containing seeds and fruit.
Its radiant color is like the bright moon, resembling the conch and the kumuda flower.
Smiling, seated upon a white lotus,
abiding in the Samādhi of Universal Observation; as for the retinue of the Lotus Family,
place the foremost one at the far west:

“Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsitātapatra Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Tārā Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Bhṛkuṭī Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Padmakulodbhava Bodhisattva, the second Śāntikarīvidyā Bodhisattva, Mahāmaṅgalavidyā Bodhisattva, Mahāmaṅgalamahāvidyā Bodhisattva, Cintāmaṇicakra Bodhisattva, Yaśodharā Bodhisattva, Stūpamahāmaṅgala Bodhisattva, and Mahāpratisarā Bodhisattva.”
Next are the Bodhisattvas Śvetapāda, Mahāmāyūrī, Jalaśrī, Amoghapāśa, Vasuparipūrṇa, Śvetakāya Avalokiteśvara, and Parṇaśabarī.
With lotus flowers, lamps, and scented ointments, these four articles of internal offering, he dispatches his retinue, as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field.
To her right is the one of great renown, the Noble Ārya Tārā;
her complexion is a blend of blue and white, appearing in the form of a woman in the prime of life.
With palms joined holding a blue lotus, his circular halo pervades everywhere;
light radiates from pure gold, and he wears a white robe with a gentle smile.
Forming the "inner bond" (*antarbandha*) with the space and wind fingers extended, Vajravārāhī stands to his left.
With hands hanging down holding a rosary garland, three eyes, and wearing a topknot;
the Honored One’s form is pure white, and the color of his circular halo has no fixed hue.
Yellow, red, and white blend together, while the mudrā in front represents the intersection of wind and fire.
Next, near Viśuddhi, one should paint the Honored One Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
his robes are the color of a conch shell, his hand holds a lotus of great compassion that is flourishing yet not yet in bloom, and he is encircled by a halo of light.
The Consort dwells at his side, known as the Holder of Renown;
adorned with all manner of exquisite necklaces, her golden body is magnificently arrayed;
holding a branch of fresh, wondrous flowers, she carries a *pātra* in her left hand.
The mudrā follows that of the Vidyārāja; the upper fingers of the wind-wheel (the index fingers) are bent.
She is near the noble Tārā and dwells upon the white Bhūtadāmara;
her hair-crown is draped in pure white, and she holds a *padma* lotus in her hand.
Concentration and wisdom merge in a vacant mind, Like space and water entering the moon.
Before the Noble One, he appears as The Great Powerful Vidyārāja,
With the color of the morning sun’s radiance, His body adorned with white lotuses.
Blazing brilliantly, he forms a wreath of flames; his roar is wrathful as his fangs emerge.
With sharp claws and the hair of the King of Beasts, his seal is like that of Śvetaketu.
Beneath the wheel of the empty wind, they are separated by a distance like a grain of wild barley.
The two earth-mandalas join at the base, and the two wind-mandalas are on their sides;
thus the vessel is formed.
The mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is: *Avalokiteśvara*.

Namo samantabuddhānām. *Svabījāt sarvatathāgata-avalokiteśvara-karuṇātmaka-ra-ra-ra-ra.* Homage to all the Buddhas. From their own seed-syllable arises Avalokiteśvara, the Lord of All Tathāgatas. "Avalokita" means the Contemplation of the Buddhas; it is the Contemplation of the Universal Eye of Equality. His essence is Great Compassion (*karuṇā*). The syllables *ra-ra-ra-ra* signify "dust" (*rajas*), which enters the gateway of the letter *a*.
Āḥ signifies "non-existence," which carries the meaning of being free from defilements; its essence consists of emptiness and compassion.

It is detached from the three poisons and attains the three roots of goodness, such as non-attachment, thereby giving rise to the three liberations; thus, it possesses the three syllables RAṂ. HŪṂ signifies "cause" and "terror"; by means of the power of great majestic ferocity and sovereignty, it terrifies the threefold veil of defilements, causing them to attain purity and become identical with the Buddha-eye.
HŪṂ: The syllable HA signifies joy; the bindu above it signifies samādhi. The four seed-syllables signify non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Alternatively, the initial syllable SA may be taken as the essence, signifying awakening. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Svalpāhārī is: *LUTARĀNI VI*.
Like a boat ferrying people across the great ocean, it places them upon the other shore where they attain mastery:
*Namo samantabuddhānām*, with *daṃ* as the seed syllable, *karuṇā-upaveśa*—that is, the one who possesses compassion.

This Bodhisattva is born from the eye of Avalokiteśvara; because he perceives the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he is named Universal Eye (*Samantacakṣus*). He perceives the essence of Suchness (*tathatā*); *tārā* (pronounced *tāriṇī*) signifies "one who delivers. The initial syllable *ta* constitutes its essence. The mantra of the Bodhisattva *Svāhā-vikūṭi* is: in Sanskrit, *Bṛhukūṭi*, which means "to terrify all" and signifies being eternally free from the four Māras.

*Namo samantabuddhānām* (1) *Bṛh-* (2) *Sarvabhaya-* (all fears) *Tāra-* (having Suchness as its essence) *Saṃni-* (also meaning "fear") *Ru-* (3) Furthermore, it has the sense of "terrifying. The seed-syllable is *sa*. *Sarvabhaya-tāra* has Suchness as its essence. *Saṃni-ru* also carries the meaning of "fear."

The former refers to having fear, while the latter refers to being fearless. Because all sentient beings possess terror and have not attained the state of fearlessness, they give rise to pride, self-clinging, and arrogance based on the conditions of dependent origination, which leads to fear. This [mantra] causes them to leave behind fear and attain fearlessness. HŪṂ SPHOTTAYA (the one who crushes and destroys obstacles) SVĀHĀ. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta is: MAHĀSTHĀMAPRĀPTĀYA. NAMAḤ SAMANTABUDDHĀNĀM.
SAÑJAÑJAYA (the one who doubly conquers). "Doubly" means: first, the conquest of afflictions (*kleśa*); second, the conquest of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Entering the gateway of the syllable A is non-arising.
Above it is the great bindu (visarga), which signifies that by removing the two obscurations, one attains the birth of Great Emptiness; it is the seed-syllable for the meaning of the immovable Sūrya.
Phenomena that move possess arising and ceasing; whether moving or unmoving, all are signs of instability.
When two dots are added to the side, it becomes identical to *nirvāṇa*, which signifies the meaning of firm abiding.
Having already abandoned the two obstacles, they are identical to the Great Void. As for the mantra of the Bodhisattva Yaśodharā, who dwells like all Buddhas in *svāhā*:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ janya-yaśodharāyai svāhā*. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Pāṇḍaravāsini is as follows: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ pāṇḍara-tathāgata-viṣaya-sambhava-padmamālini*. [Explanation: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām* (Homage to all Buddhas).

*Pāṇḍara-tathāgata-viṣaya-sambhava* (Born from the sphere of the White Tathāgata). *Padma* (Lotus). *Mālini* (Possessing a garland), meaning she enters [the mandala] with a lotus garland as an ornament for her body.

This is that which can give rise to the merits of all Buddhas, serving as the adornment of the *dharmakāya*. *Svāhā*. The mantra of Hayagrīva (*Aśvamukha*) is: *Haya-kṛ-va* (consuming ignorance and exhausting all obstacles):

*Namo samantabuddhānām* (Homage to all Buddhas). *Haṃ* (seed syllable). *Hūṃ* (terrifying). *Khaṇa* (consuming all obstacles). *Pari* (shattering). *Sphoṭaya* (crushing and reducing to nothingness). *Svāhā*. The mantra spoken by all Bodhisattvas is: *Vidyā-vihara-sthitā nāma śaśiketu-maṇḍitā-sattvāḥ*: (The Vidyā-dwelling, named the Moon-crest Adorned Being).
*Namo samantabuddhānām*. The *kṣatrantarāyana* sword mantra of Kṣitigarbha is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām hā hā hā trayaḥ*.
"Trayaḥ" refers to the causes of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.

Generally, all mantras describe the virtues of their respective deities; this [mantra] is the general description of the virtues of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. *Sutanu* refers to the "wonderful-colored body"; because his own body is utterly pure, it is called the "wonderful-colored body," which is the Dharma-body.
*Svāhā*. The mantra of those who follow the teachings is as follows: *Kiṃkara-nam*: "O Son of the Buddha, listen attentively!
Next, in the third enclosure to the east, is the Vajra Altar of Bestowing Vows, its four sides equal and perfectly uniform."
Guarding with the Vajra seal,
one generates the fire maṇḍala; within that heart, one further places a wondrous and excellent blue lotus.
Encircle it with the root mantra; according to the ritual,
arrange the seed-syllables to serve as the seeds,
and further adorn its four sides with blue lotuses.
First, one should install Mañjuśrī, his body the color of emerald;
with five topknots crowning his head, he has the form of a youth;
in his left hand he holds a blue lotus, upon which is displayed the vajra seal.
With a compassionate countenance smiling broadly, seated upon a white lotus flower,
his wondrous marks are perfect and his light is pervasive, mutually reflecting one another all around;
abiding through the empowerment of the Buddha, he is the sovereign of spiritual powers and samādhis.
And with an immeasurable retinue:
Avalokiteśvara, Samantabhadra, Abhimukha, Abhyavakāśa, Jaya, Vijaya, Jambhola, and Aparājita.
The Bodhisattva Northern Light Net, the Bodhisattva Jewel Crown, the Bodhisattva Stainless Light, the Bodhisattva Moonlight, and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī with Five Topknots.
The Bodhisattva Candrāmbujopacīṣṇi at the southern gate, the two messengers—the Bodhisattvas who follow the command and Mañjuśrī—and the four who summon according to the command.
“Join the blue lotus with the hollow center; hold the fire-wheel behind the water;
and press the two wind-fingers against the space-nail.”
Holding a net of various jewels and diverse exquisite necklaces,
seated upon a precious lotus throne, he gazes at the Buddha’s eldest son,
who holds the mudrā of the fixed-fist hook.
Holding a jewel wheel amidst fire, he wears a jeweled crown and bears the jewel seal.
His right hand holds a stainless-light lotus; it is a blue lotus that has not yet blossomed. The front seal is slightly extended and bent, like the light radiating from the Buddha’s body.
For Kicijini, hold a sword; for Prajñāmukhi, extend the wisdom-fist with the wind, fire, space, and earth fingers pressed together like a poised striking gesture.
For Upakicijini, the front mudrā consists of the fire-wheel and halberd with the space, wind, earth, and water fingers pressed together.
The earth-wisdom holds the banner seal; the fist of concentration has the earth and water fingers extended upward, while the space finger presses down upon the wind and fire.
The Citra-kumāra [seal] has the right fist as a wind-wheel staff.
Invoke the wind as the hook with the outer fist;
the inconceivable youth binds the fists internally with concentration and wisdom,
placing the space-finger upon the back of the wind-finger.
The five types of attendants are surrounded by the two assemblies; their guardians are invincible.
Mañjuśrī’s *tripuṭa* (three-fold) hand gesture joins the two fire fingers and presses against the backs of the two water fingers; the two wind fingers pinch the wheel of space.
The mantra of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is: *Oṃ jūḥ śrī-mahā-buddhāya*.
*Namo samanta-buddhānām*. *Māṃ hī hī*. Regarding the sound *ha*: it signifies being free from duality (*dvaya-hetu*) and transcending the realm of the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna-gocara*).

It is indeed the youth who dwells on the path of liberation; he has descended out of mindfulness of his original vow. He is Kūṣmāṇḍa, the youth who shatters the four Māras. He destroys all Māras. Vemucī, he is liberated. Bhaṭṭasiddha, O virtuous one, where do you dwell? It refers to the path of liberation. Smara, remember! Smara, remember! Bhaṭṭirāja, O Noble One, may all vows fulfill the deliverance of all sentient beings, no different from my own. Now, remember your former oath! Svāhā! The mantra of the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha is: *jālinī-prabha*.

To gather all sentient beings and cause them to abide on the ground of liberation, one summons the great virtues of all Buddhas; this is the meaning of the "hook" (*aṅkuśa*). *Namo samantabuddhānām*. The seed syllable is *Hrīḥ Hrīḥ*. As before, *Kumārakrodha* (The Youthful Wrathful One). *Jñeya* means knowing that all phenomena are like illusions. *Svabhāva* is the nature of all things. *Vidyadhara* means thoroughly understanding that all phenomena are like illusions and abiding within the true nature of all Buddhas. *Svāhā*. *Namo samantabuddhānām* (1) *kumāraviśvarūpagatikuṃmāra* (2) *manusmara* (4) "remember [your] vow. *Svāhā*. The mantra of Keśinī is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām* (1) *kili* (2) [seed syllable] *he he* (3) summoning *kumāri ke* (2). The youth calls out with a female voice.

The two sons are also Mañjuśrī-samaya. *Nāya* (with *raṅga* and *na*) combined, *praṇidhāna* (the vow), *smara* (remember), *prati-jānīhi* (the original vow). The meaning is: "O Venerable One, grant me the supreme vows obtained by you from Mañjuśrī. *Svāhā*. The mantra of Upakeśinī is called *Upakeśinī*: with wisdom (*jñāna*), one pierces through ignorance (*ajñāna*).

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām*, *nili* (the seed syllable), *pinaya* (piercing), *raṅga* (wisdom), *jña* (ignorance). The preceding phrase contains the sound *a*, which is connected [to the following], and thus constitutes ignorance.

The phrase "piercing with wondrous wisdom" means to penetrate non-wisdom and reach the ultimate reality. This refers to the maiden Kūmarī, whose meaning is *samādhi*. She is addressed with a feminine vocative as *Svāhā*, and the mantra of the Bodhisattva Prajñāpāramitā is called *Vasu-mati*, also known as *Dhana-prajñā*, which is the "Recollection of the Wish-fulfilling Banner."

*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ hiri smaraṇaṃ ketuṃ / By means of this banner of sublime wisdom, all Māras are destroyed; now one should recollect it so that I may likewise [attain this]. Svāhā.* The mantra of the youth Citra (or, as the original text reads, Citramīri):
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ mīre svāhā.* The mantra for summoning the youth, drawn by the hook until enlightenment: *Namo samantabuddhānāṃ mīre svāhā.*

*Namo samantabuddhānām ākarṣaya* (summon, summon; "summoning" and "invoking" both carry the sense of hooking [the deity] to come). *Svāṃ kuru* (make everything; taking, giving, and so forth are all included), meaning that whatever tasks the Venerable Mañjuśrī points out or instructs, one should perform them all. *Ārya-mañjuśrī-kāya-svāhā*. The mantra of the Inconceivable Youth (*Adbhuta-kumāra*), who manifests in a wrathful form, fulfills wishes, upholds the teachings, and brings to fruition what has not yet been accomplished, is as follows:
"The practitioner, on the left side, Next performs the one of Great Renown, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, The seed-syllable of Great Diligence."
It is said that the Cintāmaṇi jewel dwells within the wheel of fire, accompanied by a retinue of majestic and dignified forms; one should know those attendants to be:

the Bodhisattva Compassionate Pity, the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Evil Realms, the Bodhisattva Bestower of Fearlessness, the Bodhisattva Worthy Protector, the Bodhisattva Inconceivable Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Arising from Loving-kindness, and the Bodhisattva Dispeller of All Fevers and Afflictions.
“The secret symbols should be arranged in succession;
he is named the Honored One Who Removes Obstacles. Abiding in the samādhi of the power of compassion, his wisdom and merit merge with the hollow space.
Earth, water, and space enter the moon; one holds the space within the water.”
Joining both hands at the wind-wheel, like holding a maṇi jewel;
on the right of the Honored One, to dispel doubts and strangeness, form the inner fist with the fire-wheel upright,
and place a single-pronged jewel vase.
The Bodhisattva Bestower of Fearlessness raises his hand to bestow fearlessness;
his preceding mudrā is no different [from before]. The Bodhisattva Protector through Wisdom places his hand of compassion at his heart.
With the wind of wisdom, one holds flowers aloft and scatters them three times; with the rotation of compassion, one moistens and places [the hands] to the right.
With compassionate mindfulness resting upon the heart, one bends down the fingers of the fire-wheel (the middle fingers).
Dispelling all feverish afflictions,
he forms the hand of granting boons,
from which streams of nectar flow forth.
Pervading the tips of all fingers,
next is the Wisdom of Inconceivability; with the hand of Bestowing Fearlessness,
it holds a jewel in the gesture of space and wind, while the fire and other elements are slightly bent and dispersed.
The mantra of the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin is: *sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhaye*.
Through the power of mastery over the compassion of the *dharmatā*, he is able to remove the obscurations (*nīvaraṇa*) of all sentient beings and attains mastery over those obscurations.

*Namo samantabuddhānām*. The seed syllable is *sattva*. It is for the sake of the great benefit of sentient beings (*sattvārtha*). *Utpādaya utpādaya*: it causes [the mind] to arise and be generated; it opens up and makes manifest their virtuous nature. *Tara tara*: here, *ta* is the syllable *ta*, meaning "suchness" (*tathatā*).
*Raṃ* signifies "stainless. Adding a dot (*bindu*) signifies "dust," which refers to the realization of the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).

*Raṃ raṃ* means to remove the four stains: first, the stain of attachment and views; second, the stain of the Pratyekabuddhas; third, the stain of the Śrāvakas; and fourth, the stain of the Bodhisattvas. This means that by removing these four stains, one enters the stage of purity. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Vighnāntaka (Remover of Doubt and Wonder) is: *Krodha-hara*.
This translation is for the purpose of removing doubt or, alternatively, removing defilement.
When there are matters concerning which the assembly has doubts that cannot be resolved, this Bodhisattva goes there to sever their web of doubt and acts as a friend who does not need to be asked.
In Sanskrit, it is called *Hokurina* (入):
*Namo samantabuddhānām*, followed by the three-syllable seed-mantra *hasan*. *Ma-ti* means "lack of wisdom"; *che-noga* means "to sever. It severs ignorance so that wisdom may arise.

It also carries the meaning of severing and decisively cutting through, just like the meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* (the Diamond Cutter). The mantra of the Bodhisattva Abhayamdada (Bestower of Fearlessness) is as follows:
*Sarvasattvānāṃ bhayana-namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ ra-sa-na*. The three syllables are the seed-mantra. *Abhayandada* means "bestowing fearlessness."
By what Dharma is fearlessness bestowed?
It is by abiding in the letter *A*, which is free from all arising.

Venerable One, your aspirations are already fulfilled, whereas ours are not; may you grant them to me and to all sentient beings. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Sarvadurgatipariśodhana is: *Vajra-pāyañjaha*.
Namo samantabuddhānām | trimśad-abhiṣodaraṇi-jyasa-ttva-dhātu sattvadhātum |
Because all sentient beings are covered by beginningless ignorance, they constantly dwell within the three evil realms.

May the Venerable One, having attained the five powers, lift them up to cause them to ascend into purity, and cause all sentient beings to escape the triple world. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Jñānarakṣita is: *pāritraṇaśayamati*.
The left fist rests at the side of the waist;
this is also called the Wisdom of Compassion (*karuṇā-jñāna*).

*Namo samantabuddhānām vihasan*—these four syllables are the seed-mantra. *Mahā-mahā*, "the Great among the Great," *samara*, "to remember," and *pratidhāraṇa*, "to uphold"—because it intends to eliminate all suffering through its original vow, it is therefore named the Wisdom of Protection (*trāṇa-jñāna*).

Now, by calling upon his name, one causes him to remember his original vow so that he may rescue and protect all beings. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Mahāmaitreya is as follows: *Mahāmaitry-abhyudgata*: *Namo samantabuddhānām* (the seed syllable *ccham*).
*Svāhā vidu-citta-artha-abhyudgata*. [The meaning is: "Homage to all Buddhas! Svāhā! O you who have arisen for the sake of the wise mind!"
It is said that this loving-kindness arises from one’s own mind and is not obtained from another; therefore, it is called "Great Loving-Kindness" (*mahāmaitrī*).

This means it arises from the mind of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*) and does not arise from the seeds of another's mind; thus, it is said to arise from one's own mind. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Karuṇāvarta (Compassionate Revolving) is: *Mahākāruṇā-praṇidhāna*, also known as "Great Compassionate Revolving."

*Namo samantabuddhānām*. *Yam* is the seed syllable. *Karuṇe*, "O Compassionate One," for this Bodhisattva is bound to compassion and lacks autonomy; he is constantly led by compassion because he eliminates all suffering. *Mūre niṣṭhā smara*, "Remember [your] fundamental vow"; the Honored One vowed to save sentient beings, so now one should recall that original vow to protect us. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin is as follows: *Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhiṇe*. *Namo samantabuddhānām*. *Iḥ* is the seed syllable.

*Viṣkambhin*, "O Dispeller," who fulfills the vows of all sentient beings through the method of transcending causes. *Vara-pradāya*, "Bestower of Boons"—how can the unobtained boons be granted to others? How can what was previously unobtained be bestowed? How can one's own vows be conferred upon others?

The vows established by the Bodhisattva are now fulfilled; now, recollecting his original vow, he removes all burning afflictions for all sentient beings and transforms all sentient beings, causing them to attain the Buddha-way. Svāhā. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Acintyamatinandana is as follows: "Ajita-matindana-nanda:
'In the north is the Honored One Kṣitigarbha, Whose seat is most skillfully adorned;
His body dwells within a womb of flames, Upon a ground embellished with various jewels.'"
Interwoven and mutually interspersed, with four jewels forming lotus flowers where the Holy Ones dwell; indestructible as vajra,
it is the samādhi of the sphere of practice, together with great renown.
There were immeasurable retinues:

the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhādhyāśaya, as well as the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Ratnābhāsa, the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, and the Bodhisattva Sarvāśokāndhakāravidhamana.
"Secretly within, they are bound; the fire-wheels stand upright and spread apart, with the two voids holding the wind on their sides.
To the right, one contemplates the Honored One of the Jewel Realm; wisdom scatters the void, wind, and jewels, with a three-pronged mudrā atop the jewels."
Ratnapāṇi (Jewel-Palmed) holds a single-pronged vajra mudrā upon his jewel;
his wisdom-fist extends the water-wheel (ring finger) to press against the space between the third fingers.
Dharaṇīdhara (Earth-Holding) holds a jewel upon his right hand, with both hands forming the vajra mudrā.
The Ratnamudrā-hasta is the five-pronged vajra upon a jewel;
the Karma-vajra-mudrā is formed by joining the hands of meditative concentration and wisdom like a lotus,
with the tips slightly raised and opened toward the sky.
The mantra of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva is: *Vasava śapratipūraka | Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Hā hā hā trīṇi*.
This refers to the cause of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). *Vismaye* means "wonderful" or "rare."

All sentient beings are constantly afflicted by the various defilements of the notion of self (*ātman*). If one recites this mantra, the notion of self is immediately eliminated; this is rare, and it is truly marvelous. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Ratnākara is as follows: *Namo samantabuddhānām | dhanamjaye mahāmaha |* (Great among the great). *Svāhā.* The mantra of the Bodhisattva Ratnākara is:

*Ratnakara*: *Namo samantabuddhānām | dhanamjaye mahāmaha*. (Great among the great). *Svāhā*. *Note: The term "dhanamjaye" is interpreted here as a transcription of the Sanskrit "dhananjaya," meaning "Victorious in Wealth" or "Possessor of Treasure. The phrase "mahāmaha" is rendered as "Great among the Great."*

Regarding the "Jewel Place" (Ratnasthāna): just as jewels arise from within the great ocean, because they are born from that mind, it is called the "Jewel Place. Svāhā. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi is: *Ratnapāṇi*.
Jewels are born from the hand; it is said that noble beings are born from jewels.
From what jewel are they born?
They are born from the bodhicitta.
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ* (Seed syllable: *Śam*). The mantra of the Bodhisattva Ratnāvatī is: *Dharani dharāṇi*.
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ* (Seed syllable: *Dha*). *Dharāṇi* means "earth."

Because the earth (*dhara*) is able to sustain all things, it is given this name; *dhara* means "to hold. Because the Buddhas bear the burden of sentient beings, they are called "Earth-Holders" (*Dharāṇī*), and they cause sentient beings to likewise attain this state. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta is:

*Ratna-mudrā-hasta-tānām*. *Namo samanta-buddhānām*. *Haṃ* is the seed syllable. *Ratna* means "jewel"; *nirmita* means "produced by all the Jewel-Born Buddhas. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati is: *Nṛtyeśaya*. [Verse]:
"In the western direction is Gaganagañja, Vigorous and clad in white robes."
A circular, white, and pleasing maṇḍala, with a seat of a great white lotus;
holding the mudrā of the Great Sword of Wisdom, such a firm and sharp blade,
its edge as keen as ice and frost, abiding in the realm of purity.
Taking their own seeds as the seed-syllables, the wise one honors the north by arranging them thus:

"The Bodhisattva of Dānapāramitā, the Bodhisattva of Śīlapāramitā, the Bodhisattva of Kṣāntipāramitā, the Bodhisattva of Vīryapāramitā, the Bodhisattva of Dhyānapāramitā, the Bodhisattva of Prajñāpāramitā, the Bodhisattva of Upāyapāramitā, the Bodhisattva of Praṇidhānapāramitā, the Bodhisattva of Balapāramitā, and the Bodhisattva of Jñānapāramitā."

Next, place Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Susiddhikara Bodhisattva, Vajrasūcī Bodhisattva, Subāhu Bodhisattva, Vimalagati Bodhisattva, Sahacittotpādacakravartin Bodhisattva, Smṛtyupasthānaja Bodhisattva, Krodhāṅkuśa Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Amoghapāśāṅkuśa Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Sahasrabhuja-sahasranetra Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

Next are the Bodhisattvas of the Maṇḍala: Vajrabhairava Bodhisattva, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, Kuṇḍalī Bodhisattva, Amoghasiddhi Bodhisattva, Amoghapūjāratna Bodhisattva, Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī Bodhisattva, Ekajaṭā-rākṣasīrāja Bodhisattva, and Ekādaśamukha Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
“The mudrā forms are as taught in the ritual instructions; the Honored Secret One is identical to Maitreya, holding the *kṣepa* in the water with empty hands.
Next is Gaganāmala, whose two hands form the wisdom-sword mudrā.”
Gaganamati holds the Dharma wheel;
Padmavajra holds the lotus;
Viśuddhamati holds the conch.
The Lotus-Blossoming Wisdom-Practice;

Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva dwells in the Great Vajra Invincible Samādhi, which is peerless and called "Invincible" because he has realized the vajra-nature of all Buddhas and is able to uphold the wisdom of the Tathāgatas; therefore, he is named the Vajradhara. His mantra is called the Inner Fist Five-Spoked Seal, and his name is Vajrapāṇi.

*Namo samantavajrāya*. Homage to Vajrapāṇi! The seed syllable *vaṃ* refers to Caṇḍa, the most fierce among the fierce; that is to say, he who displays a form so violent and cruel that there is none surpassing him, even to the point of devouring all the world without remainder.
The character "zhàn" (戰) negates sound; it represents birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
The dot above it signifies the meaning of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*);
this expresses that birth-and-death is identical to Great Emptiness.

*Na* signifies "to fight" or "to oppose. It is like transcending birth and death to become equal to the great void; thus, there is none who can act as an adversary. *Mahāruṣṇa* means "Great Wrathful One. Because there is no one capable of opposing him as described above, he is "Greatly Wrathful. *Hūṃ* is the same as the three previous [syllables] representing liberation.
The above methods terrify sentient beings, causing them to leave birth and death and attain the three liberations.
This is the foremost fierce and violent power of all Buddhas to destroy the world and cause all to enter the Dharma-realm, returning to the Vajra-realm. The mantra of Maṅgala is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ trīṭ trīṭ traṭ traṭ*. "Traṭ" signifies the meaning of destruction; by means of this samādhi, one slays the afflictions of the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*).
In this context, the word "many" signifies equality, which is identical to the samādhi of the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
Furthermore, "ṭha" signifies the abandonment of ego-conceit (*asmimāna*); by abiding in this *tathatā*, all ego-conceit naturally ceases to exist.

To speak of it again is the ultimate meaning. *Jrayanti* means "victory," which refers to subduing all obstacles and difficulties through the dharma of suchness and selflessness, causing them to submit out of fear; this carries the sense of "battle. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Vajra-needle is as follows:

*Namo samantavajrāṇām*. The seed syllable *saṃ* [is for] all phenomena (*sarvadharmān*). *Nirvedhī* means "to pierce"; it refers to piercing through all phenomena with the needle of vajra-wisdom. *Vajrasūcī* is the "vajra-needle," the sharp and keen wisdom that contemplates and pierces the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). *Varade* means "supreme boon"; having first made this vow, may we all reach the source of all phenomena. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Vajra Chain (*vajraśṛṅkhalā*)—also known as the Vajra Conch (*vajraśaṅkha*)—the chain of great wisdom, is as follows:

*Namo samantavajrāṇām*. Homage to all Vajras; "Vajra" is the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*) of all Buddhas—a specific name for the Buddha—*Hūṃ*. The three liberations are as before: *bandha bandhaya vauṣaṭ*, like a strong man seizing a weak person.
Furthermore, it is said that one is freed from two kinds of bonds, namely the bonds of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the bonds of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
*Mavata mavataya bava*: the upper heavy bond makes [the fetters] firm;
just as severing the neck causes the body parts to be destroyed, so too are the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) shattered. *Vajranābha vai*: this is the vajra.
Born from the great wisdom of the Vajradhātu, *sarvatrāpratihata*—nowhere is there anything that can harm;
like the substance of a vajra-jewel, nothing at all can cause injury.
Because consciousness realizes this vajra-nature, *svāhā traṃ*.
The mantra of the World-Vajra is also called the Wrathful Moon-Mark (Candramas-kūṭa).

*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇām hūṃ*—“summoning and invoking,” “stainless and free from causes,” with a bindu (*anusvāra*) attached to the side, signifying extreme wrath; *hūṃ* as before, *phaṭ*, *caḥ*, *haḥ*—[subdue] all māras and obstacles! *Svāhā*. (1) Maṇibhadra Ratnabhadra; (2) Pūrṇabhadra Pūrṇabhadra; (3) Pañcika Caṇḍika; (4) Sātakarṇi; (5) Haimavata; (6) Viśvakarman; (7) Aṭavaka; (8) Pañcāla. The mantra for all the yakṣas is:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ viśramanāya svāhā*. Regarding the mudrā: join the palms with hollowed fingers, interlace the fire-fingers and space-fingers, form the two wind-fingers like hooks, and join the water-fingers upright.
One who can devour everything without remainder and is swift is called a yakṣa; they constantly devour sentient beings without ever being satisfied.
By the great vow of the World-Honored One, they constantly devour the defilements and obstructions of sentient beings, causing them to dwell within the matrix (garbha) of the Dharma-realm.

*Namaḥ samanta-buddhānāṃ yakṣa*. Here, "yakṣa" has the meaning of "vehicle," and "kṣa" has the meaning of "devouring. *Śvara* means "sovereign"; because they are sovereign over devouring all afflictions, they are so named. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the Yakṣiṇīs is as follows: With both hands, place the palms together with the earth-element fingers (thumbs) entering the center; join the earth-element fingers (thumbs) with the space-element fingers (little fingers); then interlace the wind, fire, and water fingers (index, middle, and ring fingers respectively) and spread them out, just like the *samaya* mudrā.
*Namo samanta-buddhānāṃ yakṣa-vidyādharāṇāṃ vidyā-dhara-bandha-svāhā.* The mantra for all Piśācas: *Paramārtha-satyam avikāriṇam mahā-karuṇā-duḥkhitān sattvān na parityajati:
Namo samanta-buddhānāṃ piśāca-cetana-paramārtha-gati-asamprāpta-svāhā.* The mantra for all Piśācis: *Piśāci-nī-nāma:*
"In the northeast is Īśāna, with his retinue of bhūtas and others;
the trident mudrā is formed by the samaya-fist, with the fire and wind fingers extended and their backs bent.
The mantra of the deity Īśāna, who is an emanation of Maheśvara, is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ* (the heart mantra is *ru-ve-nara*, and the name of the deity is given as the root mantra: *svāhā*). The mantra of Sarvavuda is as follows:
"Indra, Lord of the Eastern Gate, Dwelling upon Mount Sumeru, Adorned with a jeweled crown and necklaces, Holding a single-pronged vajra in his hand."
Surrounded by the hosts of devas,
within the eight-horse chariot, the two consorts stand at left and right;
Sītā and Viśītā, with Mārīcī leading the way.
The gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and the Sphere of Infinite Space, the gods of Nothingness and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception;
the deities Dṛḍhā and her consort, the deity Vajrapāṇi and his consort,
the god Madanotsava and his consort, and the two gatekeepers on the left and right.
Together with the two female gatekeepers, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Mahābrahmā, the four dhyānas, and the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens. Next, regarding the wood used for the implement:
it is made from *udumbara* wood; one should wear wet rice-colored clothing for rites of increase (*puṣṭi*), non-attachment (*arañjana*), and so forth.
The sheep, the ox, the secret, husband and wife; the comet, the falling star, and the thunderbolt;
the sun, the lord of the day, and his retinue.
Bind the hands in the inner seal of Śakra; extend the two wind-fingers like needles, standing upright in space.
The sun and moon look up at his merit and wisdom;
the waters enter the void and support him from the side;
the wheel of fire desires to stand shoulder to shoulder with him.
Relaxing the two earth wheels,
join the Prajñā and Samaya hands; the wind and earth joints face one another,
while water and fire hold each other, and space is placed side-by-side at the heart.
The nine fingers and two wings joined together, the wheel of space extended side by side.
Brahmā holds a red lotus like the moon; Samaya holds water within the void.
The consort’s wind [element] is joined with fire; Space holds the joint within water.
The Gandharva secret seal: Form the inner-bind and extend the water-wheel.
Asura uses the wisdom-hand, Twisting the wind upon the space-wheel.
The hand-gesture (*mudrā*) is like that of the deity Ghoṣadatta.
If the various devas perform the *karmamudrā*, it may also be performed with a single hand.

The mantra of Śakra Devendra is as follows (some say "inner-binding" [*antarbandha*] and join the thumbs and index fingers upright, fearing error): This is the merit of Śakra Devendra during his causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), when he extensively established the hundred-fold *pañcavārṣika* great assemblies.
The Great Donor named Śikṣa, who has attained tranquility and abandoned all defilements, possesses a naturally unborn and pure mind-ground;

he employs these to adorn his pure *dharmakāya*. The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ śrīkalyāṇavardhana svāhā*. The *dhāraṇī* of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, King of the Heavenly Kings, is as follows: Form the right fist with the *ākāśa* (thumb) extended upward like a hook, not touching the other fingers; the left hand is positioned similarly, with the wrists crossed.

*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ dṛḍha-tara-svara ra-ra-pramardana svāhā.* Adorned with various celestial garments, with his left hand hanging down holding a sword and his right palm grasping a jewel, the mantra of the Sun Deva (Sūryadeva) is as follows: The world says he acts for the benefit of sentient beings; the letter *A* is unborn. This is a metaphor for the Buddha-Sun Samādhi: when the sun rises, it destroys all darkness, and the Bodhicitta naturally opens.

Riding upon this sun of the true mark of Suchness (*tathatā*), the Honored One whose great light universally illuminates the Dharma-realm: *Namo samantabuddhānām ādityāya svāhā.* The mantra of Mārīcī is as follows:

*Namo samantabuddhānām Mārīcyai svāhā.* The mantra for the Seven Planets, the Twelve Constellations, and the Nine Planetary Spirits is as follows: Join the hands of Samādhi and Prajñā; slightly bend the index fingers (the space-fingers) and separate them from the fire-wheel (the ring fingers).

This single class of beings is neither human nor ghost, yet they are capable of causing terror to people; at times they are known as the *graha* (seizers). If one approaches the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), they become joined with them. Taking the nine *grahas* as the standard:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām*, *Arahe*, *Jaye*, *Ajite*, *Amale*, *Amṛte*, *Śvete*, *Rohiṇī*, *Mānavike*. Among the nature of the luminaries (*jyotiḥ-svabhāva*), they attain mastery (*vaśitva*). Calling upon their names, "O Masters," *Svāhā*, the Brahma-mantra is spoken: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Arahe jaye ajite amale amṛte śvete rohiṇī mānavike vaśitve svāhā ||*

*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ* (Namo samanta buddha nām). *Pra* (seed syllable), *jaya sarvasattvān pātaye svāhā*. The mantra of the Gandharva King is: "With pure and equanimous voice, producing words of exquisite melody, may all who hear it be made joyful:

*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ viśuddhārtha-svarārtha-vāk-niścāraṇa svāhā*. (*Viśuddhārtha* means purity; *svarārtha* means the meaning of sound; *vāk-niścāraṇa* means the utterance of pure speech—all of which are worldly samādhis. *Svāhā*. The mantra of the various Asura Kings is: "The letter *Ra*, free from defilement and ungraspable."
*Namo samantabuddhānām*. *Asura-rājñe rāṃ rāṃ triṃ daṃ praprasvāhā*. The mantra of the Mahoragas is called *Mahoraga*:
*Namo samantabuddhānām* *garuḍa-vilambasvāhā*. The mantras of all the Kinnaras are called:
*Namo samantabuddhānām* *hakasāna-vihāsāna-kinnarāṇāṃ svāhā*. The mantras of all humans are called *Manuṣyāṇām*.
*Namo samantabuddhānām*. The mantra of the Universal Consort (Viśvamātṛ) is: *Viśvapramardane svāhā*. The universal seal (*viśvamudrā*) is: *Namo samantabuddhānām*. The seed syllable is *Lu*.

*Kaloka* means "the world" (*loka*), which signifies "darkness. *Kara* means "to do. *Sarvadeva* means "all the gods. *Nāga*, *yakṣa*, *gandharva*, *asura*, *garuḍa*, *kiṃnara*, *mahoraga*—these and all other classes are subsumed.

*Haridāni*: [This refers to] you. *Namo samantabuddhānām*. The mantra of the Universal Consort is: *Viśvapramardane svāhā*. The universal seal is: *Namo samantabuddhānām*. The seed syllable is *Lu*. *Kaloka* means "the world," that is, the sense of darkness. *Kara* means "to act. *Sarvadeva* means "all the devas. *Nāga*, *yakṣa*, *gandharva*, *asura*, *garuḍa*, *kiṃnara*, *mahoraga*—you and all these various classes are gathered here. *Haridāni*: [This is] for you.
Cittakalasa: *cittam* refers to the heart;
*aṣṭau gaṇān saṃgrahya* means having gathered the eight classes [of spirits] and so forth; *vicitragati* means various destinies; *svāhā*. "Lord of Secrets!"

These are the seals of the foremost Tathāgatas, arising from the faith and understanding of the Tathāgatas; these foremost seals, as described above, extend from these [initial ones] down to Ḍākinī as the last.
If one were to exhaustively enumerate their categories and retinues, their number would be boundless, as described in the extensive version consisting of one hundred thousand verses.
This present version mentions only their leaders; yet, just as grasping the main rope of a net captures the whole, these are the insignia of the Bodhisattvas, and their number is immeasurable.
Furthermore, O Lord of Mysteries!
You should know that even the movements, gestures, and postures of the body are all secret mudrās.

The manifold speech produced by the faculty of the tongue should be known as mantras. If an ācārya clearly understands yoga, deeply penetrates the secret intent, and is able to purify the bodhicitta—because his mind is pure, he masters the secret dharma—then whatever he does is for the benefit and subduing of sentient beings. Whatever actions he performs accord with the majestic deportment of the Buddha; there is not a single movement or gesture of any part of his body that is not a secret mudrā, and every word he speaks is a mantra.
Therefore, O Lord of Secrets!
Those bodhisattvas who practice the bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras and have already resolved their minds upon enlightenment (bodhicitta) should abide in the stage of the Tathāgata;
the ācārya must thoroughly understand the methods of the maṇḍala, mudrās, mantras, and so forth. First, [he should...]

First, by not violating the Dharma rules, practicing the contemplative exercises of yoga for a long time, purifying the actions of body, speech, and mind, and embodying an understanding of the practice of the three secrets of equality—one is identical to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
When principle and phenomena do not conflict, one skillfully knows the sequence and does not err; you should know that such a person will certainly attain great benefit without fail.
If one differs from this, it is equally a slander against all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and a transgression of the samaya;

such a person will certainly fall into the evil realms. It was for the sake of universally causing all sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision so that they may all become like me, that the Tathāgatas established this Dharma-seal through skillful means as their fundamental vow.
Just as in the world, the stern edicts and commands of a great king cannot be transgressed, for those who do so will surely incur severe retribution;
you must likewise follow the scriptures and diligently seek the Dharma of the sutras, and further consult an enlightened teacher so as not to deceive yourself.
If one does not follow the Dharma, one’s efforts will be in vain, time will be wasted in vain, and nothing will be accomplished; one will only incur guilt and derive no benefit.
Regarding those things suspected of being impure: Visualize the syllable *raṃ* burning them all away;
Having performed the empowerment for the sake of accomplishing the task, One may eat according to the light of the Ten Powers.
"Purifying the mind while performing recitation, before the count of meritorious practice is finished,
one should not allow interruptions midway. Whether it be through speaking,
needing to go out, or due to negligence, do not let the count remain incomplete."
One will then lack accomplishment.
With the syllable *ḹ* at the tip of the tongue, or by practicing the Mother-mantra of the Vajra Family,
even speech shall not create an interruption.
The rest is as in Susiddhi; for each and every mantra, perform mental recitation (manas-japa).
With inhalation and exhalation as the two, remain constantly in the primary union.
The letter A is distributed throughout the limbs.
Having maintained this for three hundred thousand recitations, Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī,
and the Vajradhara noble deities will appear before one and touch one’s head with their hands.
The practitioner should prostrate in salutation and swiftly offer arghya water.
Mentally creating incense, flowers, and garlands, one immediately attains purity of body.
When the allotted time for recitation has ended, place the rosary in its proper location and enter *samādhi*.
After a duration equal to a meal, emerge from concentration.
Again, having bound the root mudrā and recited the mantra seven times,
next arrange the Akṣobhya-locana [mudrā], offer incense, flowers, and so forth,
with pleasing and sublime verses, as well as the argha offering and the making of vows.
To speak of the empowerment of the Savior, so that the path of the Dharma-eye may pervade everywhere and endure for a long time:
one should join the vajra-palms and touch the body everywhere while reciting the vidyā-mantra.

One hundred thousand is one *lakṣa*; one million is one *koṭi*; one *koṭi* is one *ayuta*; one *ayuta* is one *nayuta*. As explained at length in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the mantra for the empowerment verse says:
“O Great Protector, difficult to endure! Unravel the great boundary by circling to the left;
Re-presenting the *samaya*, Disperse it above the crown of the head.”
Directing the mind toward the noble deities, prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground,
and address the assembly of noble ones: "To all the Tathāgatas currently present,
and to the world-saving Bodhisattvas who maintain the uninterrupted teaching of the Mahāyāna."
To those who have attained the state of excellence,
I pray that the assembly of noble devas will definitively bear witness to me; may each of you remain at your ease as you wish,
yet return again out of compassion.
The mantra says: "As before,
with the protection of the three secrets, performing confession, rejoicing, and so forth,
contemplating the bodhicitta, one abides in the body of a sattva."
Sustained by the power of the Sage, and because one’s conduct accords with one’s vows,
one upholds the teachings transmitted by the Vidyādharas.
Without transgressing the samaya and practicing in accordance with the precepts, siddhi shall manifest before you.
Relying upon the teachings of Mahāvairocana, I shall reveal the practices of the yogins;
through the cultivation and realization of these supreme merits, may all sentient beings be universally benefited.

*The Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra-vikurvāṇādhiṣṭhāna-padma-garbha-bodhi-dhvaja-cihna-sāmānya-mantra-kośa-siddhi-yoga*, Volume Lower. The *Mahāvairocana-siddhi-yoga* in three volumes was compiled by the Dharma Master Fǎquán while residing at Qīnglóng Monastery; therefore, it is called the "Qīnglóng Monastery Ritual Manual" (*Qīnglóng-sì Yíguǐ*).
This [text] was brought here at the request of the three masters Jikaku, Chishō, and Yūei.
However, regarding the edition now being carved into woodblocks, it has not yet been determined which master’s original version this is.
If one follows the *Annenroku*, which states, “Yūei’s version is the same as the previous one, differing only in that it contains annotations,” then it would be the original version of Sōe.

If one relies on the words "kha na kha" inserted within the speech of all Vajra-Commanders, it is said: "These four characters are added according to the Sūtra"; this is the root of the realization of wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding the five-character verses, the old edition had four lines per stanza, whereas this version has been revised to three lines per stanza, as intended in the *Xuanguiji*.
Moreover, where the collation remains unsettled, annotations have been added at the head to await future scholars.
Recorded by the śramaṇa Huiguang of Lingyun Temple in Wucheng on the twenty-first day of the month of Mṛgaśīrṣa in the year of Renchen, the second year of the Zhengde era.
